in California should be a man of unusual capabilities and energy. the

Myron English Smith was born in Dixon, Illinois, on December 2,
1906, where he lived until completing . his public school education in
North Dixon High School. He then turned west to attend the Unive.r~
sity of California at Los Angeles where he became an active member
of the Debating Team while earning his B.A. degree which he received
in 1929. Law School then beckoned him and after studying at the Law
Schools of Stanford University and the University of Southern Califo.r~
.
nia, received his LL.B. degree from the latter in 1932.
After passing the State Bar the same year. he entered private practice
for two years. It was inevitable, howev~r. that his ability was soon to
attract the attention of corporation officials. and in 1934 he joined the
staff of the Union Oil Company in Los Angeles, and he today is the
Treasury Attorney of that great California corporation.
In 1934 he was married to the gracious and charming Katherine
Joplin, who endeared herself to all as the First Masonic Lady in Cali~
fornia during the Grand Lodge year. They have an ideal family-two
boys, Myron English Smith, Jr., and Gregory Newcomb Smith, and a
daughter, Sandra Kay Smith. Myron, Jr., a Mason, is serving in the
U.S. Navy in the Asian theatre of activity, while Gregory. very recently
raised by his Grand Master father in his father's lodge, is completing his
education at U .S.C. Sandra is completing her senior year in Pasadena
High School. They have an equally ideal family home in the foothills
of Sierra Madre, a suburb of Los Angeles.
Grand M aster Smith was raised in University Lodge No. 394 in
Los Angeles (now in Torrance) on July 23, 1928. His devotion to the
ideals of Masonry, soon recognized by his brethren. resulted in his being
elected Worshipful Master in 1941. He also served as a member of the
Board of Trustees of the Los Angeles Board of Relief from 1941-1943.
Grand Lodge, too, soon became aware of the many capabilities of this
most genial brother and he was soon active on important Grand Lodge
Boards, serving for three years on the Board of Directors of the UCLA
Masonic Clubhouse, 1947-50, and for nine years (the constitutional
limit) on the Board of Directors of the Masonic Homes of California,
1949~58, the last four years serving as Vice President. In 1961 he was
appointed Grand Orator and his remarkable ability as a fluent and
thought-provoking speaker immediately brought him acclaim throughout
the jurisdiction. It was not surprising, therefore, that the brethren elected
him as Junior Grand Warden in 1962 and that he progressed through
the chairs to become our 1OOth Grand Master in October, 1965.

In my "fight talk" to you as Masons this day. I want it clear 1 am ~ot
interested in Masonry that sits back and lets the world go by. I am interested in Masonry that is striving for victory of truth over falsehood.
for victory of humanity over inhumanity, for victory of justice over injustice, for victory of love over hate. There is a game to be played and a
world to be won , for a specific training instruction I would call you to
live in the example of The Temple Builder-King Solomon. First, he
was a learner; second, he was a builder.

puter." Yesterday looking out at the Golden Gate Bridge, I couldn't help
going through the same ritual again, "What do I see when I see the
Golden Gate Bridge?" The answer came, "I see God. "

Masonry, on the playing field of life. is always at it's best illuminating and illustrating The Truth of God. This is our greatness! When a
Mason is learning his degree work he is active and at his best, when an
officer is learning his ritual work he is active and at his best. it is when
a Mason stops learning he becomes an "inactive." I feel drastic measures
must be taken in Masonry to keep our members learning . I would suggest
every Lodge break it's total membership into groups which will meet at
least once a month for the study of the tenets of Masonry. This is my
proposal to activate the inactive.
How tragic is the cartoon showing a man standing in a library surrounded by shelves of books . he is looking out the window-it is raining.
Underneath is the remark, " What on earth can a man do on a day like
this?" My. fi~ht talk would dare every Mason to "look around you."
there are hm1tless resources at your disposal, there are limitless possibilities for your life!

HE w AS A LEARNER

Let's fac~ it! Daily there are those who "give up" in the learning
struggle, their stand~rd answer given in various forms to the problems of
the world ~ w.~ether 1t be automation. racial riots, or wa r in Viet Nam) is
an apathe.t1c what can I do about it anyway?" In giving up his identit
as a learning, purposeful individual he becomes like the young lady wh~
went up to th~. bank window with a check to be cashed and was asked
b?' the ~eller, Can you .identify yourself?" The girl. flustered by this,
~1pp~d 1~to he~ purse, quickly ~ulled out a small mirror and glancing into
it sa~d, Yes, 1t s me all right. · The greatest danger of the automation
age is that man will give up his learning and forget who he is and who
created him.

King Solomon was known by men far and near for his great wisdom.
He was one who listened and learned from people of other lands than
his own. He was a king who could see in the common-place affairs of his
people The Truth of God illustrated. The kind of lea~n.er that I. would
call you to be is one that likewise is able to see the spmtual behind the
material.
Walking with a friend the other day we p~~sed a neighbor's garden
filled with blooming roses. My friend asked, What do you see when
you see a rose?" I answered hurriedly, "Something very beautiful." He
went on. "I see God." His reply, a simple ritual of awareness, has stuck
in my mind. A week later while going through a large company building
I was shown their newly installed I.B.M. computer. Suddenly I found
myself asking the question "What d.~ you see wh~n you see .an l:B.M.
computer?" My answer came back, I see a creation of mans mmd, a
mind that was created by God. "I see GOD when I see an I.B.M. com-

To practice learning by awareness I would suggest every Mason play
the game "Katzenspeil" (cat's play). A cat can see in the dark and we
unobservant mortals ref use to see, that is the basis of the game. Dr. Marcus Back tells of first learning the game from his cousin Herr Dokter
Paulu~; he tells that when his stern, German~trained, cousin came to visit
at their home. he had a way of turning the living room into a classroom
One evening the Herr Dokter called all of the family together, it wa~
then he annou~ced he wo~ld .t.each the game of "Katzenspeil." Ordering
all to close their eyes he said, Now while your eyes are shut I want each
of you to describe the room we are in. What are the walls like? What is
~e pattern of the curtains? What color are the carpets? What are the
titles of the books on the shelves?" Then changing, "What are the colors
of the clothes. of tho~e sitting ne~t to you?" Needling and prodding he
made the family realize they didn t know the answers, all were living in
a house with details and treasures that had never been noticed. The Herr

Dokter then becoming philosophical said, "how can we have the kind
of world we would like to have?" His answer was a definite one. "take
a n inventory of the kind of world we've got."
The truth hits home! We fail to see our blessings. w e do not observe
that we already possess many of the things we desire. This applies not
only to material things but to our philosophies and beliefs as well. Such
a game should startle every Mason to awake to the truth in symbols and
in allegories that surround him. My plea is "come alive Masons to God's
Truth illustrated all around you!"
At a recent convention held in the East a famed speaker left his
startled listeners with this awakening fact, "There are fifty-two million
more people born into this world each year, one hundred thousand more
every twenty-four hours. Unless something is done to check the growth
of population or expand the world's food production, racial starvation is
inevitable. I don't know what you are going to do with the rest of your
four score and ten , but I am going to be seeking answers. Good night,
sleep well, a nd if you can't sleep--get up and do some more searching."
Masonic Brothers, we walk in the footsteps of King Solomon who was
a man of wisdom, of grea t learning. Let us come alive to our purpose. let
us recommit ourselves to the discipline of great learning.

President Gene Bartlett of the Colgate-Rochester Divinity School
tells the story of Wahlstrom, a thinking kind of man. It seems that
Wahlstrom purchased an old bomb sight, he took it apart to see what it
w~s like but when he started to put it together again he added some
m1~cellaneous parts. He became fascinated with his new pastime and
neighbors began to bring in parts of machinery for his use. He went on
expanding his mechanism, for ten years he kept putting together wheels,
cogs, belts and bolts. As a result he had a machine called "Wahlstrom's
Wonder." When he threw a switch three-thousand parts began to move
~ells rang, lights flashed, belts from large wheels ran small wheels'.
There is only one difficulty," said a friend of Walhstrom, "it doesn't do
anything ...it just runs. It is a monument to trivia, it is creativity that goes
nowhere.

HE WAS A BUILDER

King Solomon will be remembered in time and eternity as the Builder
of The Temple in Jerusalem. He was more than a dreamer and a thinker,
he was a man of action. He showed by his life that work is a compliment
to awareness. he truly projected his awareness of God into every day
·r eality.
The example of King Solomon is needed as we see our own disconnectedness in thinking and action. I recall the story of a man's visit to a
business executive friend . As he walked into his friend 's office he looked
around and said, "What happened to all of the THINK signs you h.ad
posted?" The friend answered," I had to take them down, for the people
in the office were sitting around thinking all day and nobody was doing
any work." The other extreme is the statement made "he is so busy being
busy he can't get anything done." We would underscore that thinking is
not enough without building, and building is not enough without thinking.
A large industry in California was looking for a creative executive
to take over one of it's important departments. One of the questions
asked of the applicants interviewed was "have you ever built a bridge?"
Those who gave an immediate "no", or who laughed the question off.
were marked off the possibility list. Those who pondered the question
and said in their own way "yes, I have tried to build some bridges along
the way-between my wife and myself, with the kids, with neighbors,

greatness is exemplified not by what is written on his resting place, but
by what he himself did not write for it. Calling his daughter to him he
told her that only the following inscription (and not one word more)
was to appear. "Here lies Thomas Jefferson, author of the Declaration
of Independence, of the Statutes of Virginia for Religious Freedom, and
father of the University of Virginia." That is all!
Jefferson was Governor of Virginia, you recall, he doesn't mention
this; he was elected to Congress-no mention; he was appointed Minister to Frnnce-not a word. Jefferson was Secretary of State, he was Vice
President-no word; and, oh yes, a grateful Republic elected him President of the United States-twice. He does not mention that at all. Why?
Jefferson told his daughter why. "Things that are not on my inscription,"
he said, "are things the people did for me. The things that are on it are
things I did for the people."
My final question I would put to each one of you personally as a
Brother Mason is, WHAT WILL YOU DO FOR THE PEOPLE?
This query is to hold up the Masonic dimension. You are called to build
the temple right where you are in the midst of a society of people. Look
again to King Solomon, he declares all of this by his example as a learner
and as a builder.
Finally, as your sipiritual coach I would "give you hell" as a team, to
go out on the field of life and play to win-play every minute as a team.
May the spirit of the living, loving Supreme Grand Master of The Universe inspire you.

smiles we long" but with Whittier we must add "But God has led our
dear ones on. And He can do no wrong."
The statistics of our report can be given very briefly. During the
year four hundred and forty of our members were translated from our
imperfect Lodge to the "Celestial Lodge above where the S upreme
Grand Master forever presides." Of these, three were Masters of their
Lodges at the time of death; five were Wardens. and four hundred
thirty two were Past Masters. Three hundred fourteen Lodges suffered
losses. Two hundred fourteen Lodges lost one member each; seventy
one Lodges lost two; twenty four Lodges lost three; and three Lodges
lost four.
On the roll this year are the names of many men distinguished both
in the Fraternity and in our State. During the year we lost three of our
Past Grand Masters. Oscar Lawler, elected Grand Master in 1908 and
our Senior Past Grand Master, passed away January 3, 1966. An
eulogy for Brother Lawler will be presented by Past Grand Master Leo
E. Anderson. Past Grand Master Frank Harwell, Jr., whom we had
hoped would be with us for many years. was taken from us on January
26. 1966. An eulogy will be given by Past Grand Master Guy B. Mize.
Past Grand Master Leon 0. Whitsell, well known historian of Masonry
in California, died February 26. 1966. An eulogy for Brother Whitsell
will be given by Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderson.
The list of those who have held some office in this Grand Lodge
is unusually long . All merit mention but. owing to the number involved,
the space given to each will have to be limited in order to keep wi thin
the time assign~d for this report. In some cases the Lodges have not
provided information and we shalf be limited to what we can get from
office records.
Claude. Everett Cole. Sr., whose name ought to have appeared last
year, passed away June 4, 1965, at Redding. the victim of a heart attack.
He was born on May 23, 1906, in Los Angeles, and graduated from
Inglewood High School and studied at U.S.C. and U. of C. at Redlands. For many years he had his own accounting firm in Inglewood.
He was active in civic affairs and was nominated for the "Man of the
Year" in his community. In 1964 he moved to Redding and acquired a
partnership in a mortuary there. He was raised a Master Mason on
October 10, 1927, in Inglewood Lodge No. 421 and served as Master
of that Lodge in 1959. He was also active in York Rite and a member
of Scottish Rite. Brother Cole served on Grand Lodge committees and
for two years was Chairman of the important and active Public Schools
Committee. An active Mason, he will be missed especially by his brethren in Inglewood and Redding.
Arthur Bridge Ste.el was probably the senior member of this Grand
Lodge at the time of his death on October 16. 1965. Born in C ambridge,
England, on May 8, 1870. he came to California at the age of sixteen.

Again we have reached the hour when we pause to take note of
those of our members who have been taken from us during the past
year, and to pay our tribute of respect and affection to their memory.
Death is an inevitable experience for everyone. "Man that is born
of woman is of few days and full of trouble. He cometh forth like a
flower and is cut down; he Heeth also as a shadow and continueth not."
The roll of the deceased in an organization with the number of members of this Grand Lodge is inevitably long. None of us will know all on
that roll but all of us will know some of the names. and some of us will
recognize many names of long time friends and brothers with whom we
have worked and had rich fellowship. The compilation of the list. as
reports come in from the constituent Lodges, is always a little sadden~
ing. We do not "sor·r ow as those without hope" but we miss the companionship we have enjoyed. While it is a joy to meet many friends as
we assemble at Grand Lodge, and to feel the warm handclasp of many
we have known across the years, we do miss some whom we looked
forward to greeting. '"We long for household voices gone. For vanished

Clouds B. Sylvester, well known Methodist Minister, was released
from the body after a long, lingering illness on November 26, 1965, at
the age of 86 years. C.B. was born in Brookville, Indiana. and was educated at Moores Hill College. now Evansville College, Indiana. He
became a Methodist Minister in 1901 and came to California in 1907.
He was for forty years an active Minister a nd served a number of
churches. including Modesto, Burlingame, San Jose, Berkeley and
Stockton. Retiring in 1946. he made his home in San Jose and for seven
years after his retirement served as Associate Minister at San Jose Firs t
Methodist Church.
He was made a Master Mason in San Jose Lodge No. 10 and was
a member of that Lodge until his death. In 1950 he served with distinction as Grand Chaplain of this Grand Lodge with Past Grand Master
Arthur Paulsen. A member of San Jose Cons istory, Scottish Rite, he
was coronated 33° in 1957. A man of great heart a nd booming voice.
he was a powerful spea ker. He was respected by all and loved by those
of us who knew him well. His work here is finished a nd he has entered
into the joy of his Lord.
Joseph Russell Know/and. When Joseph R. Knowland succumbed to
pneumonia on Februa ry 1, 1966, at the age of ninety two years. California and the United States lost a truly great and distinguishe d citizen .
In our limited space we are able to say little about one about whom so
much has been written . He was born in Alameda on August 5, 1873.
educated in Alameda schools and at University of Pacific which was
then in San Jose. Elected to the State Assembly at the age of 25, he
served also in the Sta te Senate. Appointed to Congress in 1904, he was
afterward elected for five full terms. He was influential in the development of many projects- the Panama Canal; the construction of Oakland
Harbor; the San Francisco-O akland Bay Bridge. A great conservation ist, he served as Chairman of the State Park Commission from 1937
until he retired in 1960. He had much to do with the growth of our

State Park system. In 1915 he became Publisher of the Oakland Tribune and has been a potent figure in journalism across the years. It is
impossible to enumerate the committees for social betterment on which
he has served. One writer says. " Knowland packed more accomplishments into his 92 years than a half dozen other distinguishe d men might
have done."
Joseph Knowla nd was raised a Master Mason in June, 1898. in Oak
Grove Lodge No. 215 and was Master of the Lodge in 1904. He served
as Grand Orator in this Grand Lodge when Edward H . Siems was
Grand Mas ter in 1948. Very active in Scottish Rite, he was coronated
33° in 1937. He was also a Knight Templar and member of many social
and service organization s. His son, William F. Knowland, was for many
years a U .S. Senator and Senate Leader of his party. He is now Editor
and Publisher of the Oakland Tribune. Joseph Knowland is also survived by a large number of grandchildre n and great grandchildre n.
No words of ours can add luster to the life of this great man who
did so much for his State and fellow men. He will be greatly missed but
we are deeply thankful for the achievemen ts of this outgoing life, and
are enriched by so much that he did.

Edward Leslie Kellas was the victim of a heart attack on June 2,
1966. at the age of seventy three years. Brother Kellas was a native of
Newton, Kansas, and had lived in Fresno since 1905. A graduate of the
University of California and a respected member of the bar, he was
appointed to the Superior Court bench in 1949 by Governor Earl Warren and was re~~lected without opposition in 1950, 1956 and 1962.
Edward Kellas was raised a Master Mason in June, 1934, in Fresno
Lodge No. 247 and was Master of his Lodge in 1947. He served on the
Committee for M asonic Education from 1963 until the time of his death.
He was also Grand Bible Bearer in 1964.
Roy Harvey Parkinson was gathered unto his fathers on March 3,
1966. A nati ve of Ashland, Oregon, he was one of several brothers who
became doctors. His particula r field was eye, ea r, nose and throat and
he practiced in that field for many years in the East Bay a rea. He was
raised a Master Ma son on November 21, 191 7, in King Solomon's
Lodge No. 260. In 1920 he demitted from tha t Lodge and affiliated with
East Bay Lodge No. 489 where he went through the chairs and served
as Master in 1926. He was commissione d Inspector in 1928 and served
for eight years on the old Dis trict 33. His death at the age of seventy
five ended a life which had shown a high degree of devotion to Masonic
activities. One of his services. typical of the man , was the ca re he provided, without cha rge. to the residents of the Masonic Home at Decoto,
who were in need of the help he could give. He is survived by his wife,
a daughter, and a brother - also a doctor. We pay our tribute of respect to a brother who served long for the joy of serving.

The complete list of the 440 is attached to, and made a part of this
report. Many merit mention. Some have been men of many talents who
have served in high places and whose names are well known. Some were
men of fewer talents whose names are not known outside their own
areas, but who nevertheless served up the measure of their strenHth and
ability. All kept alive the imagery of Masonry in California and mai ntained standards of integrity. brotherly love, charity, and truth, so
essentially necessary in this modern age. Their work was not finished .
God having provided that we must have a part in their tasks. May all
of us, as a fitting tribute to their memory, rededicate ourselves to the
task of maintaining the great principles of Masonry in every phase of
our modern life. Today we do not sorrow for the dead but gird ourselves anew in the faith that death is not a "grim tyrant" but a " kind
messenger"; not a punishment but a blessing; not an end but a beginning. and in that faith let us press on with strength in the work to which
God has called us.
"Inasmuch as their labors were not in vain in the Lord."

FRANK HARWELL, JR.
By Guy B. M1zE
"Thus severing another link in the fraternal chain by which we are
bound together."
Once again these familiar words from our memorial service for departed brethren were brought home to the hearts of the Masons in this
jurisdiction when the sad news of the passing of Past Grand Master
Frank Harwell. Jr. came to us on January 25, 1966.
Following the Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge in October. 1965, he returned to his home and business in Los Angeles, but we
who had occasion to be in contact with him were distressed to learn that
he was not his usual dynamic self. A rest of several months and treatment for a heart condition seemingly were restoring him to good health.
but shortly after returning to his office a sudden and final attack claimed
our Brother while he was seated at his desk in his office.
Funeral services "vere conducted in the presence of a large gathering
of friends and Masons in All Saints Episcopal Church, Beverly Hills,
by its ministers-Dr. Kermit Castellanos. who ser\'ed this Grand Lodge
as Grand Chaplain during Brother Harwell's year as Grand Master. and
by Dr. G. Herbert Smith. Brother Harwell was an active member of
All Saints Church, serving for many years as a vestryman and he had
rendered distinguished service to the Episcopal Diocese of Los Angeles.
Frank Harwell. Jr. was horn October 4, 1898 at La Grange. Georqia,
the son of Judge Frank Harwell, Sr. and Ruth Lovejoy Harv.1 ell. He
attended the pubtic schools in La Grange and then went on to the University of Georgia. There, he was a member of Kappa Alpha Fraternity
and of the class of 1920. Following graduation, he enlisted in the United
States Infantry and served as a Second Lieutenant during World War I.
Following military service, he married Virginia Boston of Marietta,
Georgia, who survives him together with three married daughters and
six grandchildren who were his great delight. He is also survived by two
brothers and two sisters.
Frank Harwell's business career "vas in investment banking-first in
New York City, then in Atlanta, Georgia, and, from 1927 on, in Los
Angeles, where he was well known and respected in the investment
banking world. At the time of his passing , he was a general partner in
the firm of Lester Ryans & Co.. with which firm he had been associated
for a long number of years.
Shortly after coming to Los Angeles, Frank Harwell evinced an
interest in Masonry which was to play an important part in his life for
the remainder of his years. He became a Master Mason in Beverly Hills
Ledge No. 528 on April 23, 1929 and, after service in several stations.
was elected Master for the year 1935. In September, 1936. he was
appointed Inspector and continued as such until April. 1948 when he

28

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

was appointed Assistant Grand Lecturer. It was only natural that he
would advance for his ritualistic and administrative abilities pointed him
out as one of our leaders-then , and of the future. Special committee
ass ignments and service on the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes
of California also claimed his attention.
In October, 1950, Frank Harwell was elected Junior Grand Wardi:-n
and he advanced each succeeding year until October. 1953 when he
became our 88th Grand Master. A reading of the 1954 Proceedings
provides evidence of the year of service rendered and of the progress
made under his leadership. Among other things . we are deeply indebted
to him for the authorization to the Correspondence Committee to begin
the publication of the California Freemason as the official quarterly magazine of the Grand Lodge of California.
Appointed to the Finance Committee upon completion of his term as
Grand Master. he continued to render distinguished service for eleven
yea rs as its chairman and, during the same period. as a member of the
In vestment Committee of Grand Lodge .
A member of the Los Angeles Scottish Rite Bodies. and of other
organizations, Frank Harwell chose to devote his talents to his Blue
Lodge and to Grand Lodge. Possessed of a keen mind. his counsel could
always be depended on. His was the faculty of giving full attentio n to
whatever the problem might be which was placed before him. Willing
to disagree. if need be, his reply would always be in the interest of the
fraternity as he saw it. Constructi\'e in his thinking . his labors bore fruit
for our fraternity.
Yes. we will miss his keen insight, his sage advice. his jovial camaraderie and, above all. his great love and respe ct for the traditions. the
tenets and the landmarks of Masonry, plus his willingness to do everything in his power to uphold them in all their strength and glory.
Frank Harwell was a staunch American who served his country; a
devoted husband and father to whom love for his family was paramount;
a master craftsman who learned well the use of the Plumb. Square and
Level; a Master who wielded the gavel in true Masonic fashion; a
Brother who understood a nd practiced the teachings of Masonry.
At the 195"1 Communication, the Grand Chaplain , the Very Reverend Kermit Castellanos. chose as the subject for the dev otional service,
these words. "The Spirit of Man is the Candle of the Lord.'' And it
was about the spirit of man upon which he dwelt in his remarks-the
spirit of man in his personal life. in his business life. in his fraternal life.
in his spiritual life. And it was pointed o ut that you cannot examine the
spirit of man - but you can sense it.
So it was with Fra nk Harwell. He was a man of spirit. It was not
difficult to sense the na turalness of the spirit which was within himthe spirit which motivated him to furnish his brethren with the example
of a true Master Mason- a Master Mason whose spirit remains with us
as a candle to help light the path of Masonry for all time to come.

During the course of the Annual Communica tion the Grand Master
from time to time called on various distinguishe d guests to address the
members of Grand Lodge. In addition to expressing his appreciation for
being present, each in his own way discussed Masonic subjects of interest. The talks were humorous, provocative and thoughtful. The Grand
Lodge responded with standing ovations following each of the messages.
On Monday afternoon Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith proudly
introduced his son, Gregory. probably the youngest Mason in a tte ndance, who received his Third Degree during the prior month. The Grand
Master expressed pride and happiness in his son becoming a Master
Mason and particularly because he was privileged to confer his son's
First and Third Degrees.
On Tuesday afternoon the Grand Master presented Brother John
M. Gordon, who gave the report of the Endowment Board. In presenting
Brother Gordon. the Grand Master stated that he was retiring as Chairman and expressed the appreciation and than ks of all Masons in California for his many years of service and devotion to the Fraternity and
to the Masonic Homes endowment program . He asked that this a ppreciation and thanks be extended to Brother G ordon's wife. Margaret,
who has been his able assistant. Following the report of the Committee,
the assembled delegates rose in appreciation .

My Brethren , welcome to the One Hundred Seventee nth Annual
Commun ication of the Grand Lodge of Californi a.

MEMOR IAL SERVIC E

"Stretch ing before us lies the coming year
as pure as snow,
Where no foot has set, fresh fallen from heav'n
to earth below;
We tremble: ere we tread on ought so fair,
and so unknown ,
And dare we, seeing not whereto it leads,
set out alone?
Go thou before, Great Guide and Spirit,
Counsell or Divine;
So shall we make no footprint s of our own,
But tread in thine."
Author unknown .
In this spirit, twelve short months ago we began in this place the new
Grand Lodge Year. And now we: gather 'round to review together the
events of the year, to survey the general condition of Masonry in this
jurisdicti on and to glean from our travels and experien ces new wisdom
for future years.
Ralph Waldo Emerson raised the: question in one of his essays :
"What is the best day of the year?" His answer: "Write: it on your
heart that every day is the best day of the year." We are meant to be
alive: all the time. and to make every day full and rich with promise, and
if today is not rich in experience, then tomorrow will be empty of any
hope or promise:.
Annivers aries are special days. So are days of annual conferen ce.
They bring to us perspective: and new vision. They remind us that time
is God's gift. The gift of life is a gift of time; it is a gift in time:; it is a
deposit in the: bank of God. And each of us each day receives the same
deposit: Twenty- four hours, no more no less. How precious it is! And
how fleeting! Man is responsib le for the stewards hip of time.
Stewards hip[ All of life is a stewards hip, a trust from God, for which
we are: accounta ble to the Great Architec t of the Universe . Our work
together as Masons is a special stewards hip, for through it we remind
one another that every man is a child of God and therefore of supreme
worth.
In humility, the passkey of spiritual life. I give you this annual report of Masonic stewards hip. Of necessity, it seeks to be succinct, pithy
and direct-t o summari ze and highligh t events, experiences, observa-

Fundam ental to all Masons is our belief in the immortality of the
soul. Each of us must recogniz e that, here and now. we are a part of
eternity. During the year we have been saddene d at the loss of many of
our brethren who were: called to the Great Grand Lodge: on High. But
we know that their spirits live on in " that house: not made with hands,
eternal in the heavens. " Our lives have been made more: meaning ful by
the fact that, for a little while, they walked with us and we: shall ever be:
inspired by the memory of them. To emphasiz e the spiritual concept of
Masonry . I asked our Grand Chaplain and the Chairma n of our Necrology Committ ee to participa te together in the Memorial Service this
morning. We are grateful to them for the lovely and beautiful tribute
they have presente d. And we express our gratitude for the inspiring
eulogies given by Leo E. Anderso n, L. Harold Anderso n and Guy B.
Mize in memory of three of their brother Past Grand Masters : Oscar
E. Lawler, Leon 0 . Whitsell and Frank Harwell, Jr.
APPRE CIATIO N
Great enterpris es require managem ent. No man can do such a task
alone. Many are engaged in it. Co-opera tion and togethern ess are fundamental in Masonry . We are: bound up together "in the bundle of life."
To the great aompany of Officers, Inspecto rs, Committ eemen, Past
Grand Officers, Masters, Warden s and Past Masters who compose the
Grand Lodge, I express deep apprecia tion for all their thoughtf ul courtesies and co-opera tion. A host of names could be given special mention.
Collectively, I thank one and all.
So vast and so great is the scope of the activities of the Grand Lodge
that an ever-incr easing degree of teamwor k is essential on the part of
the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, and the: Senior and Junior
Grand Warden s as your elective, progress ive line officers. In this respect,
the rapport has been superb and my heart goes out to Laurence E. Dayton, John F. Porter and Eugene S. Hopp, affectionately known as "Larry,
John and Gene," for their devoted service to the craft. It is my fervent
belief that. through the knowled ge and experien ce they have gained this
year, their leadersh ip will bring increased benefits to our Grand Lodge
each successive year.
APPOIN TMENT S
At the 1961 Annual Commun ication Grand Lodge adopted a report
by a Special Committ ee on Committ ee Structur e which obligated the
incoming Grand Master to appoint at least two new members to each
Grand Lodge committe e whose membership is seven or more and one

40

41

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRl\ND LODGE OP Ct'\LIPORNIA

new member to each committee whose membership is five (excepting
the Committees on Ritual. Taxation, Retirement Plan. Insurance and the
Constitutional Boards). It was also directed that these appointments be
in addition to the required appointment of a Senior and Junior Warden
to each Standing Committee. In addition, it was specified that no chairman of a committee should serve as chairman for an aggregate period
of more than ten years.
In the spirit and in the letter. I sought to implement this policy for
the first time in October. 1965. Almost without exception the affected
brethren responded graciously and rare was the instance in which a committeeman resisted replacement by a new appointee. In those few cases.
I reminded the brother that no man owns a Masonic Office and that the
office seeks the man.
In the application of the 1964 appointment legislation for the first
time, I have reached the conclusion that the formula adopted is too severe
and, if continued indefinitely, may deprive the Grand Lodge of needed
experience and wisdom in the committee personnel. Followed implicitly.
the rules will result in a complete change of committee membership during a span of three years, which I deem too drastic. Important as it is
to bring in new men, this should be accomplished on a more gradual but
nevertheless continual basis. To put the rules in better balance, therefore.
the following recommendation is made:

available to one who is searching the California Masonic Code
for the answer to a problem. I believe that our entire law should
be contained in one volume. I have no definite recommendation as
to how to proceed with such a project. I merely want to comment
at this time that, as time goes along, the need for modernization
of the California Masonic Code becomes more pressing."
To carry forward these objectives, I appointed this year a Special
Committee on Definition of Committee Responsibilities and Code Review
to:
"1. Define the duties and responsibilities of the various committees and boards of the Grand Lodge, including any necessary
job descriptions.
2. Clarify and correlate the language of the California Masonic Code for the purpose of eliminating duplications. contradictions and inconsistencies. so that it may be easily read and
understood by its users. particularly those without legal training.
The objective is not to change the basic law but to express it in
more understandable terms."
Recognizing that this task could not be completed in one year and
that two or three years' work would be involved, I asked Laurence E.
Dayton, John F. Porter and Eugene S. Hopp to serve with the others
appointed on the Committee. The project is well under way and good
progress has been made, but it is apparent that the work cannot be done
by correspondence alone and periodical conferences of the Committee
will be required. I therefore offer:

REcOMMENDATION No. I

I recommend that beginning in October. 1966. the incoming Grand
Master appoint at least one new member to every Grand Lodge Committee whose membership is seven or more and that to every Grand
Lodge Committee whose membership is five there be appointed at least
one new member in alternate years. all other aspects of the 1964 action
on committee structure to remain unchanged.

COMMITTEE RESPONSIBILITIES AND CODE REVIEW

action and inclusion in the California Masonic Code." Concerning the
Code itself. he said in his Observation No. 7:
"It has been my experience this year in much reading of the California Masonic Code that the time is rapidly approaching when
there should be an updating of our Code. Two things are necess~ry. One is to eliminate from the Code those items of duplication and of obsolescence that quite obviously need not be in the
Code. Secondly. our present Code refers, in many instances, to

dental expense of the Committee and for t,r avel of the members to a
minimum of four committee conferences during the year.
INSPECTORAL APPOINTMENTS
Under the law of our Grand Lodge it has been the duty and
responsibility of the Grand Master to appoint Inspectors of the various
Masonic districts. In making such appointments, I have considered the
recommendations of the Assistant Grand Lecturer for the particular
division and the Grand Lecturer, and in each instance did follow recommendations. although the final judgment has been mine. for which
I accept full responsibility.
In arriving at my decision, I have required that the Assistant Grand
Lecturer and the Grand Lecturer certify to me that the Brother recommended is in fact qualified in the ritual of the. several degrees. When it

42

came to my attention that men were being recomme nded to me who were
not at the time proficient in the ritual of the three degrees. I re-emph asized the requirem ent of ritualisti c proficiency prior to appointm ent. If
a qualified Brother were not available in a given district, it has been my
expresse d willingne ss to designat e an Acting Inspecto r on an interim
basis. I have always held the office of Inspecto r in high esteem and
that a Brother must be qualified in the ritual before he is deservin g of
appointm ent as an Inspecto r.
During the year W. Ben Sorrells retired as Assistan t Grand Lecturer of Division 6 after many years of faithful service. I appointe d as
his successo r, and the man in my opinion best qualified, William H.

SUSPEN SIONS FOR NON-P AYMEN T OF DUES AND
ADVAN CE REMISS ION OF DUES
A study of the past ten years has revealed that 12,987 members of
the Lodges in Californ ia and Hawaii have been suspende d for nonpayment of dues and during the same period only 3,480 have been
restored to membership. The members suspende d represen t more than
all the brethren raised in a two year period.
To develop an increasin g awarene ss and concern, in March I wrote
to all Masters and Secretari es requestin g that each Lodge establish a
full time delinque nt dues committee charged with the responsib ility of
investiga ting every instance of delinque nt dues to the end that suspensions be reduced to a minimum. At the same time, I also cautione d against
unnecess ary advance remission of dues and called attention to the observation made by Past Grand Master Theodor e Meriam in his 1965
message when he said:
"A review of the members hip returns over the past several years
reflects a steady increase in the number of instances where the
Lodges are granting advance remission of dues to a dispropo rtionate number of their members ."
In the month of May, I notified the Lodges that a prelimin ary report
indicated there would be a loss in members hip this year and urged that
in each Lodge several brethren be asked to call on a delinque nt brother
before suspendi ng him for non-paym ent of dues.
As will appear from our Grand Secretar y's Report to this Annual
Commun ication, there is a net loss in members hip this year of 1,014
members. I firmly believe that more careful investiga tion and consider ation of the reasons for delinque ncy in dues and discussio n with the individual members involved will result in a decrease in suspensi ons for this
cause. To achieve this construc tive goal I propose:
RECOMM ENDATIO N No. 3

I recomme nd that legislatio n be adopted which would provide for

GRAND LODGE. OP CALIFORN IA

the establish ment of a year around delinque nt dues committee in each
Lodge to work closely with the Master and Officers in a continuin g
effort to reduce to a minimum suspensi ons for non-paym ent of dues.
ITINER ARY
As reflected in the calendar of events attached to this report. throughout the year there have been a host of ceremonies, visitation s and functions on the official itinerary . Without exceptio n, every effort was made
to accept all invitatio ns from those in authority for the dedicatio n of

other public buildings . In some instances it was necessar y that two teams
of officers conduct ceremon ies on the same day in different parts of the
jurisdiction. There is every indicatio n that the Grand Master's itinerary
will continue to expand each year.
The enthusias m with which the officers and members of the constituent Lodges have participa ted in events for and with the Grand
Lodge has been a constant inspiratio n. The warmth of hospitali ty on the
part of all of the Lodges where ceremonies took place has been wonderful and all are to be commen ded for their devotion to Masonry .
Visits to the more remote sections of the jurisdicti on were particularly inspiring , as was the opportun ity to conduct a ceremon y at a place
or in an area where the Grand Lodge had not been for many years, or
at all.
For the reassura nce of those of our members who may not be acquainted with the officers of the Grand Lodge, may we remind you that
each is a member of a constitue nt Lodge. As such, he welcomes the

shown it to be particula rly warm in outlying areas. On every hand we
encourag e invitatio ns to your Grand Lodge Officers for fraternal visitations and ceremonies.
HAWAII

Although Californ ia chartere d Hawaiia n Lodge No. 21 in 1852, it
was not until 1878 that a Grand Master made an official visit to the
Islands. With the advent of improved transpor tation, annual visits to
our Island Lodges have long been customa ry. Each year the Grand
Master has returned with only the highest praise for our Island brethren and their devotion to Masonry . This year was no exception .
Mrs. Smith (Kay) , our son (Greg) , and daughter (Sondra ) found
that our trip to the Islands exceeded every expectati on. From the moment of our arrival, when we were greeted in tradition al Hawaiia n
manner with a total of thirty-fiv e beautiful floral leis placed upon our
shoulders, until the "Aloha" of our departur e, our brethren of the
Islands and their families were magnificent. In turn, each of our ten
Lodges on the four major islands. and the Honolulu bodies of the York
Rite, the Scottish Rite and the Shrine, De Molay, Job's Daughte rs and

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Rainbow Girls outdid themselves with their thoughtfulness and gracious
hospitality.
While all of the functions attended on the Islands are deserving of
special comment, I mention three in particular: The authentic Hawaiian
Luau prepared by our Junior Grand Steward, George Kahapea. and his
family at Honolulu Lodge No. 409 on July Ist, and two memorial wreath
ceremonies in which I participated - one at Punchbowl Cemetery in
Honolulu on Sunday, July 3rd, under the auspices of Hawaiian Lodge
No. 21, and the other sponsored by Pearl Harbor Lodge No. 598 on
July 4th on the memorial superstructure erected above the sunken U.S.S.
"Arizona" in Pearl Harbor.
While in the Islands, I learned that some of our brethren there have
been giving thought to the possibility of undertaking the formation of a
Grand Lodge of Hawaii. Whether or when such a step might be feasible
was the subject of considerable conjecture. As a safeguard against hasty
or ill considered action on the part of three or more of the Lodges, I
asked that the Inspectors and delegates of the Island Lodges meet yesterday with the Chairmen of the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy
and General Purposes, and Finance, and our seven elected Grand Lodge
Officers, for a briefing session on the burdens, duties and responsibilities
incident to formation of a Grand Lodge. Our hope is that the information shared will prove helpful to the Island Inspectors and delegates in
shielding their Lodges from over-zealous pleas for a separate Grand
Lodge until the day arrives, if it does. when the growth in membership
on the Islands might be sufficient to establish a Grand Lodge of Hawaii.
Meantime, we have urged that there be no hesitancy or reluctance in
seeking advice and guidance from the proper officers of our Grand Lodge
whenever needed or desired.

EXPEN DITUR E OF FUNDS
During the course of the year. it has become increasin gly apparent
to me that in the constitue nt Lodges much doubt and uncertain ty pr~
vails concerni ng the proper expendit ure of Lodge funds. Such matters
as the extent and frequenc y of expenses of officers for attendan ce at
dinners and meetings of District Officers' Associat ions and Boards of
Relief frequent ly give rise to problems for our Lodges. The available
sections of the Californ ia Masonic Code leave much to be desired, for
such guidepos ts as it contains are far from complete. I have been particularly concerne d by a question presente d by two Lodges which want
to know whether Lodge funds may be used to defray expenses of Inspectors for attendan ce at the Annual Commun ication of Grand Lod ge.
Apparen tly this question has not previous ly been passed upon. Inquiry
througho ut Southern Californ ia reveals that many Lodges long have
made it a practice to make substant ial contribut ions toward the expense
of their Inspecto rs when attendin g Grand Lodge, though our Code appears to contain no explicit authority for such use of Lodge funds. I
have been cautione d that to rule adversel y against the practice could
result in consider able hardship or inconven ience and might even prevent
some from attendin g Grand Lodge.
Those observat ions lead me to the conclusion that a compreh ensive

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORN IA

47

study and review of the whole subject of expendit ure of Lodge funds is
needed.
Added to this, I find that there also are areas of uncertain ty concerning the expendit ure of Grand Lodge Funds.
To illustrate , while the Finance Committ ee of the Grand Lodge is
charged with the responsib ility of preparin g an annual budget, once the
budget is adopted its duties cease and we seem to have no dear-cut
legislatio n governin g the proper expendit ure of the budgeted funds. The
funds of the Grand Lodge Me trust funds and their use should be regulated with precision and exactnes s. My attention has been directed to
inequities in the defraym ent of expenses of various committe emen when
attending Grand Lodge. Some committees, with apparent good reason,
schedule meetings during Grand Lodge Week with conseque nt reimburseme nt to their members of expenses incurred while attending Grand
Lod~e. while others do not.
When in Hawaii, I was confront ed with the necessity of approvin g
the expense account of an Officer's Coach for travel to a school of instruction on another island (even though such a school was held on his
own island) where he had been im·ited to attend upon the assuranc e
that he would receive reimburs ement. By contrast. I have been informed
that other Officers' Coaches travel equally far in Californi a to schools
of instructio n without reimburs ement.
In another area. a recent practice was brought to my attention which,
if carried to its logical conclusion. could result in a consider able increase
in the budget of this Grand Lodge.
An Assistan t Grand Lecturer approved and submitte d an invoice for
the expenses of a Past Grand Lecturer whom he had invited to a Division Conferen ce. When the invoice was question ed, it was learned that,
for the preserva tion of unity in the ritual, this was thought to be a proper
expense of the Grand Lodge. However . if such practice be continue d
across many years and if other committees and boards adopt a practice
of defrayin g the expenses of former Officers, Committ ee or Board members at their meetings , the resulting cost to the Grand Lodge could be
substanti al. Neverthe less, I authorize d payment of the charges.
With this backgrou nd, I submit:
RECOMM ENDATIO N No. 6

I recomme nd that the Finance Committ ee of the Grand Lodge be
requested to make a compreh ensive study and review of the whole subject of expendit ure of Lodge Funds and Grand Lodge Funds witho ut
being limited to the above illustratio ns and to submit its findings and
recomme ndations at the next Annual Commun ication.
Implicit in this recomme ndation is the fact that the committe e will
need to request assistanc e from other committe es and boards in developing its report. If budgetar y provision is required for meetings of the

PROCEED INGS OP THE

Finance Committ ee in preparin g its report, I recomme nd an appropri ate
provision.

CONDI TION OF MASON RY
Through out the jurisdicti on our Brethren continue to be concerne d
about members hip statistics , and properly so, for records reflect not only
a decrease in membership but an elevation in the average age of members. Encoura ging, however , are some indicatio ns that the average age
of applican ts for the degrees may tend to be somewh at lower than in
previous years.
While importan t, we should not put undue stress upon the subject
of members for the trend is not peculiar to Californ ia nor to Masonry
in particula r. Other Grand Lodges long have recorded far greater declines in members hip and even some churches have reported decrease s.
This year members hip in The Southern Californ ia-Arizo na Conferen ce
of the Methodi st Church declined from 265,387 to 263,943, a net loss
of 1,444; and in Northern Californ ia-Nevad a Conferen ce the same denominati on experien ced a similar decline this year from 130,788 to
130,149, a decrease of 639. The trend reflects, I believe, the momenta ry
preoccup ation of many people with material or transitor y interests, as
distinguished from the spiritual and eternal values of life. It illustrate s
the necessity of rededica ting ourselve s all the more earnestly to the practice out of the Lodge of the great moral and spiritual virtues inculcate d
in it.
The true estimate of the conditio n of Masonry is to be found in the
response of its members toward humanity 's crisis. That our world today
is not in good health is readily apparent . Its ills a re innumera ble and
many people are confused , uncertain and perplexe d. For some, the
dynamic developm ents of our age have produced a new intensity in their
faith in God. Others have reacted in the reverse and found their faith
ebbing away. Still others have drifted back and forth from faith to lack
of faith.
For us, as Masons, this is and should be a great time to be alive.
A period of crisis is a time of great creativity . It is under the s tress of
pressure s that the great creative advances of mankind have come. A
period of crisis invariabl y drives men back to fundame ntals. Superficial-

GRAND LODGE OP Cl\Ll t'ORNll\

19

ities will not do. And above all else a period of crisis demands our best.
During the early part of this year I emphasiz ed three factors that
make Masonry such a great institutio n: The devotion, the responsib ility
and the faith of our members . As the year progress ed I have come to
emphasiz e that which is at the very heart of Masonry : The word "love."
It is the great need of our day.
The condition of Masonry . the health of Masonry , is to be measured
and determin ed by the presence in the hearts and minds of its members
of love-lov e of God and love for their fellow men. By its presence
in our lives we are continua lly reminded of the spiritual nature of Masonry. In the words of Paul in First Corinthi ans, Chapter 13, from
which came the perambu lation of the second degree, if we have not love
we are " ... become as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal."
In the 12th Chapter of the Book of Judges. the Bible relates the story
of the Ephraim ites who, when they attempte d an escape over the Jordan
River, were challeng ed: "Say now Shibbole th." Because they" . .. could
not frame to pronounc e it right .•. " the Gileadite s knew them to be
enemies and the Ephraim ites perished at the hands of the Gileadite s.
For Masons and all mankind this is a day in which we must pronounce or perish. The word we must pronoun ce is love, a consumi ng
concern for one another, by radiating it in every waking moment of our
lives.
This is the challeng e before M asonry today. Most Masons are meeting that challeng e and, to that extent, the condition of Masonry in this
jurisdiction is good. I pray that every Mason may meet the challenge !
And, now, as we approach the conclusion of this Masonic year, I
thank you for tlie privilege of serving you. I pray for each and every
member that deep and abiding sense of love which comes from God and
commend each to the kind care. love and protectio n of all Master Masons
whithers oever dispersed .

E. SM I TH

M YRON

PROCLAMATION- DEMOLAY W EEK
MARCH 14-18, 1966
"The world goes forward on the feet of its youth. Where
those feet will lead the world is determined by what road they
walk now, with us adults."
We of the Masonic Fraternity have an obligation to the youth of
our land, to help them become the finest citizens they are capable of
becoming-just as we seek to be exemplary citizens.
The Order of DeMolay is one of the most effective means through
which to achieve this goal. A fraternal organization for boys between
the ages of 14 and 21 y ears , it was founded in 1919 by a great and good
Mason-Frank S. Land.
DeMolay's "object is the encouragement and development of good
citizenship and sound character among youth, teaching clean, upright
living by inculcating and teaching the virtues of comradeship, reverence.
Jove of parents, patriotism , courtesy. cleanliness and fidelity. Its supreme
effort is to create leaders and develop character"-so greatly needed to
lead the world tomorrow.
I call upon every Master Mason in this great jurisdiction to devote
an increasing portion of his time and talents to the continued growth and
development of DeMo!ay in California and Hawaii.
To this end, I proclaim the week of March 14-18, 1966. as DeMolay
Week in this jurisdiction and urge that each constituent Lodge and all
Masons use it to further the work of the Order of DeMolay.
I direct tha t this proclamation be read at the next Stated Meeting of
each Lodge, and, if possible, that it be included in the Lodge bulletins
for March.
Dated: January 25, 1966
Fraternally,
MYRON E. SMITH
Grand Master
Attest:
EowARD H. SIEMS
Grand S ecretary

PROCLAM ATION
FORTY-S EVENTH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

Our nation was founded upon the concept that man's rights come
from God. that man forms his governm ent to protect those rights and
that an enlighten ed citizenry is essential to the exercise of such rights.
To enlighten the people, our forefathe rs esablishe d the great America n
Public School System for all children.
The public school is an extension of the home. The success of the
public school hinges upon the continuin g cooperat ive interest and concern of the school administ ration, the teacher, the student and the parent.
The objective of the annual Public Schools Week Program is to
rededica te ourselves toward the continua tion and perfectio n of our Public School System. Through our Public Schools Week Committee, many
splendid suggestio ns are made available to each local Lodge Committ ee
to assist them in planning a program to fit the need of the local community. It is my hope that every Lodge will participa te in the local
Public Schools Week Program in such a way that every home will be
ever conscious of the kind of training children are receiving .
I. therefore , proclaim the week of April 25 to April 29 to be Public
Schools Week and direct all constitue nt Lodges in Californ ia and Hawaii
to actively participa te in an appropri ate Public Schools Week Program .
I also direct that only Stated Meeting s or those for Public Schools Week
Observa nce be held during this period.
This Proclam ation is to be read at the March and April Stated
Meeting s.

OF CALIF ORNIA

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER

MYRON E. SM !TH
GRAND MASTER

PROCLAMATION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

A grateful people has enshrined the Constitution of the United
States in the National Archives Building in the Nation's Capital. Encased in glass and sealed in helium it is displayed daily for all to see.
It can be quickly lowered manually or by an electrically operated
mechanism into a fireproof. shockproof, bombproof vault beneath the
floor. To stand before it is an unforgettable experience- for here is our
charter of freedom , the heritage and pride of the American people.
Four inscriptions adorn the entrances to the Building:
STUDY THE PAST
WHAT IS PAST IS PROLOGUE
THE HERITAGE OF THE PAST IS THE SEED THAT
BRINGS FORTH THE HARVEST OF THE FUTURE
ETERNAL VIGILANCE IS THE PRICE OF LIBERTY
This is the message for all Masons. for all citizens: The Constitution
of the United States is a living, vital thing! To create it for us our forefathers pledged their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor. We
must protect and support it with equal devotion to reap for ourselves
and our children's children the harvest of liberty and freedom it guarantees.
I. therefore, proclaim the month of September, 1966, to be Constitution Observance M onth and direct all constituent Lodges in California
and Hawaii to hold public ceremonies during that month, commemorating
the signing of the Constitution on September 17, 1787.
Also, I direct that this proclaimation be read at the August and
September Stated Meetings of each Lodge.
Dated: June 1, 1966
MYRON E. SMITH

Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

G rand Secretary

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge P . & A. M. of California:
I take pleasure in presenting my third annual report as Grand
Treasurer.
The financial stz tements and audits of the Grand Lodge, Masonic
Homes of California and the California Masonic Memorial Temple are
a part of this report. Each gives a complete financial history of its
individual corporate activity and together they represent the financial
story of the Grand Lodge and all its components. A careful reading of
the several reports, including schedules and exhibits attached thereto.
is strongly urged.
It was again my pleasure to sit in with representatives of Lybrand,
Ross Bros. & Montgomery. and with members of the office to review
the details of the audits. All appropriations and disbursements as provided in Section 191 C.M.C. were carefully reviewed by the professional
auditors . The budget approved at the last Annual Communication has
been strictly followed.
Steady and consistent progress is being made toward the objective
of simplification and coordination of the opera tion of the Grand Secretary's office. The Grand Lodge of C alifornia and its constituencies have
grown to very sizable proportions. Grand Lodge can be proud of the
Grand Secretary and his office staff. The responsibilities of the office are
very considerable and are efficiently carried out. Likewise, the committees who meet in the Grand Secretary's office, and who give so much of
their time, are wo_rthy of special commendation.
The Grand Master was requested and did authorize supplemental
appropriations to cover items totaling $31.874.76. The year under review
presented a number of unusual items , the cost of which were not completely anticipated in the budget, the larges t of which wa s the setting-up
cost of preparation for mailing the California Freemason. Reference to
these supplemental approvals will be set forth in the report of the Finance
Committee.
I am pleased to report, however, that as your Grand Treasurer, I
have kept in close touch with this program. The excesses have, in my
judgment, been justified, and are essential. It is a lso my considered
judgment that some of these are non- recurring.
Figures taken from the Grand Lodge budget, starting on Page 263
of the 1965 Proceedings, may be helpful:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

FEES FOR DEGREES

This is the first year since 1941 that we have shown a net loss in
membership. There are a number of causes immediately responsible for
this situation. Our Lodges accepted 754 fewer applications tha n a year
ago. This in itself accounts for approximately three-fourths of the loss.
Our affiliations from other jurisdictions were the lowes t they have been
since 1960-with the exception of the fiscal year 1963-when we had
seven less affiliations.
Deaths this last fiscal year were the highest of any yea r in our history-having reached a total of 5,365. T his was an increase of 357 o ver
the preceding year. The average increase in deaths for the past l 0 years,
over the preceding y ear , has been about 140 per year.
An interesting observation is that between the years 1931 and 1941
we lost a total of 16,580 members. In 1942 we sta rted to gain again
and have shown a cons istent g rowth. The addition of 117,730 members
since that time has almost doubled our membership.
Suspensions for non-payment of dues continue to increase. w her eas
the number of dues remissions a re declining . This situation seems to
evidence a certain inconsistency. If a Brother is a ctually in financial
trouble, his dues should be remitted r ather than to take the easy way
out by suspending him. Our suspensions for non-payment of dues over
the past ten years have increased in excess of 30% .
In times as prosperous a s these such increases may indicate that the
delinquent dues committees in some of our Lodges may in themselves be
a bit delinquent. We can point with pride to certain Lodges with no dues
delinquencies, no suspensions for non-payment of d ues. a nd only a minimum of remissions. A review of this program by the officers of each of
our Lodges could make a real difference. I submit this summary on
memberhip for your careful and serious study.

GRAND LooGE PERSONNEL HISTORY

In 1965. I reported on the progress made in establishing a G rand
Lodge personnel history file. The program has proven its wor th in many
ways. Even though time has not permitted the office staff to ma ke the
records as effective as they ultimately will be, their value has been shown
many times . For the fir st time in the history of this Gra nd Lodge. we
have a fair idea of its s trength- as set forth on the records filed by the
individual members of Grand Lodge. As a part of the Election C ertificate
each year, we will include a new personnel history card for the new
Junior W ardens. In this manner, we will be able to keep the reco r d
current. If more than one officer is new in the Warden or Master group.
the Lodge should request a dditional cards. We solicit your continued
cooperation. This additional information has not been available heretofore in the membership records.
At present. a study is under way to determine the most effective way
to classify the information. Our Deputy Grand Master, the Senior and

Junior Grand Wardens have found the records most helpful in their
planning for the future. For the present the records are segregated by
Lodges, Divisions and Districts. We are pleased to note the information
in the file has also proven helpful to a number of leaders in communities
throughout the State.

CALIFORNIA FREEMASON

Your staff is continually working on methods to improve and simplify
office procedures-always bearing in mind the necessity of maintaining
adequate controls.
You will note on all supply items (as we reorder them ) an effort is
being made to give each a form number for easy identification. O ur
printers are requested to show on the last order the number of items
printed and the date. In our supply room we maintain a running inventory of all items.
This year. for the flrst time anywhere we believe, we relieved the
Secretaries of the 711 Lodges of the detail and responsibility of filing
an Annual Returns Form. Instead the Return was prepared in the Grand
Secretary's Office based upon the information taken from the Monthly
Returns. As a first effort. all agreed that it worked remarkably well. It
saved much effort and time in our office as well. The statements were
prepared by l.B.M. equipment in conjunction with our over-all modernization program.

When first undertaking the task of mailing the California Freemason
to all Master Mason members of California and Hawaii Lodges, there
were many groans-principally from the Secretaries-beca use of the
anticipated additional work load. Current responses indicate that it was
not as difficult as originally antcipated. In fact, many Secretaries report
the results have been helpful in keeping their membership addresses current. We are grateful for their fine cooperation. A poor address results
in non-delivery of the magazine to the addressee. It also adds a substantial cost to distribution. In order to make certain that mailing addresses are current, Additions or Changes, or Deletions to the lists
should be in the Grand Secretary's office in accordance with the schedule
on the Instruction Sheet inasmuch as publication dates have been determined.
FRATERNAL VISITS

Our Grand M aster, Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith, arranged for
Mrs. Siems and me to accompany him and Mrs. Smith to the Annual
Communication of the Grand Lodge of Michigan on May 23-25 inclusive. It was also my pleasure, as an initial experience, to attend the
Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge of Washington and the
Grand Lodge of British Columbia in June of this year. Our Junior Grand
Warden, Eugene S. Hopp, accompanied by Mrs. Hopp and their daughter Joy were also guests of the Grand Lodge of Washington.
At its Annual Communication in November, 1965, the Grand Lodge
of Nevada celebrated 100 years of existence. Because of the dose relationship between the Grand Lodge of California and the Grand Lodge
of Nevada, arrangement was made for the elective Grand Lodge Officers
to be present. All were formally received in a group. It was an outstanding Masonic meeting.
These visitations were rewarding experiences. The hospitality of
the several Grand Lodges was appreciated. I was the principal speaker
on the occasion of a special Secretaries' meeting of the Lodges in Washington. The subject of my talk was "Membership Records of the Grand
Lodge of California." The sharing of ideas with other Grand Lodges
is worth while, and I am grateful to our Grand Master for the opportunity to attend these Annual Communications.

CONCLUSION

My sincere thanks and appreciation for the splendid cooperation of
the many Brethren called on throughout the year-the Inspectors, Lodge
Officers, Committeemen and especially the Secretaries-who have a
continuous direct·contact with our office.
My special thanks to the Grand Lodge Office S taff. It is a real
satisfaction to work with such a fine, loyal and dedica ted group of
employees.
Speaking for our entire staff, we appreciate the privilege which has
been ours to work with, and for, the Grand Lodge leadership. Our
Grand Master, Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith and his corps of
Officers have been an inspiration to all of us.
This is the culmination of another very busy year for F reemasonry.
Our special thanks to the more than 2-13 ,000 Masons in California and
Hawaii for the opportunity to serve you.

Grand Secretary

The Lodges are reminded, too. that the $25.00 contribution to the

National Memorial. and the present $9.00 contribution to the California
Masonic Memorial Temple. are covered by Grand Lodge law and are

of its by-laws.
Your Committee especially commends those Lodges which have
brought their by-laws up to date by adoption of the present Uniform
Code of By-Laws in toto. These are the by-laws of the Lodge. whether
adopted by the Lodge or not (California Masonic Code, Section 340);
and when they have been completed and adopted recently the officers.
in conducting their Lodge. may with fu!J confidence refer to the information they contain.

and resolutions, and we move the adoption of this report.

We wish to emphasize the importance of a Lodge taking im mediate
action by voting on a petition for restoration . The Committee has pointed
out many times in the past that although Grand Lodge is not bound by
the vote of the former Lodge we are influenced by it. The Com mittee
must consider many factors such as the gravity of the offense, the leng th
of the expulsion and the rehabilitation and present attitude of the petitioner. It must also consider that restora tion by the Grand Lodge does
not automatically restore the petitioner to membership in his former
Lodge. An adverse vote by the Lodge is therefore an important, alt hough
not totally determinative, factor in our decision.
We have carefully considered all the petitions and we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: that the petitions for restoration in the following trial
records be granted:
No. 1577, Hawaiian Lodge No. 21
No. 1820, Solano Lodge No. 229
and that the petitions in the following trial records be denied :
No. 1469, Mount Olive Lodge No. 506
No. 1560, La Mesa Lodge No. 407
No. 1637, Inglewood Lodge No. 421
No. 1792, Elysian Lodge No. 418
No. 1761, San Leandro Lodge No. 744
No. 1772, Pyramid Lodge No. 562
No. 1853, San Gorgonio Lodge No. 668
No. 1863, San Francisco-Vic tory Lodge No. 360.
Adopted.

ACTION BY GRAND LODGE
The Committee on Grievances reports as follows : Twenty-eight trial
records have been referred to our Committee and twenty-two of them
are considered in this omnibus report. The others will be covered by
special reports which will be given by members of the Committee.
Once more we urge the Lodges to see that copies of charges filed
are sent at once to the Grand Secretary. and that forms for proceedings
be obtained from him. All the trial forms which are in the main book
of the Masonic Code have been repealed and the standardized forms
furnished by the Grand Secretary should be used.
When charges are filed with a Master and they state a Masonic
offense he should proceed at once as directed by our Code. An unpleasant
job should be done as promptly and as carefully under our law as possible.
In Trial Records Nos. 1880, 1881. 1882, 1883, 1884, 1885, 1886.
1887, 1889, 1890, 1891, 1892, 1894, 1895, 1896, 1897, 1898, 1902. 1903.
1904, 1905 and 1906, we find that proper procedure has been followed.
that the results are supported by the record in each case, and that there
are no miscarriages of justice.
Deeming himself disqualified, Brother McCourtney did not participate in the discussions or decisions in Trial Record No. 1898.
We offer the following resolution :
RESOLVED: That in each of the trial records above-mention ed
the action taken and the result thereof be ratified, approved and confirmed.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORDS Nos. 1469, 1560, 1577, 1637, 1761.
1772, 1792, 1820, 1853, AND 1863
Petitions for restoration have been referred to the Committee on
Grievances in the foregoing trial records.
In two cases, Nos. 1560 and 1761, the petitioner has failed to first
notify the Lodge which expelled him as required by Section 767, C.M.C.

TRIAL RECORD No. 1875
The accused , a member of Moneta Lodge No. 405, was convicted of
one count of bigamy and four counts of forgery in the state courts, and
was committed to a correctional institution. Notice of intended exp ulsion
under Section 732 C.M.C. was given by the Lodge.
The accused plead not guilty and wrote a letter demanding a Masonic
trial which was set for July 22, 1965. The accused wrote a number of
letters stating he would be released from the correctional institution the
forepart of September and asked that the trial be continued for sixty
days so he could personally appear and present facts showing his innocence. His request was denied and at the trial he was not presen t or
represented.
He appealed and your Committee felt that a reasonable continuance
should have been granted to enable him to present his defense. Accordingly the purported expulsion of the accused was reversed and the matter remanded to the Lodge with directions to retry the case after a proper
summons was served. New charges, consisting of one specification of
bigamy and four of forgery. were filed and the accused was properly

82

PROCEEDING S OF THE

served. He appeared at the trial without counsel. claiming he had been
unable to obtain one, and after some proceedings the matter was continued to enable the accused to secure counsel. On reconvening it appeared that the accused was still unable to obtain counsel and the trial
continued with the accused representing himself. The accused was found
guilty on all specifications and the penalty fixed at expulsion. The
accused has again appealed.
Your Committee feels that the accused was given every opportunity
both to procure counsel and to present all of the facts favorable to him
in defense. His trial was fairly conducted and the procedure was correct
in every detail. There is no basis for further proceedings . We, therefore.
offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D: That the finding of guilt and the expulsion of the
member of Moneta Lodge No. 405, F. & A . M .. are ratified, affirmed
and approved.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1888
The accused, a member of Heritage Lodge No. 764, was charged
with two counts of unmasonic conduct in that he had stated to several
brethren and written a letter to the Secretary of his Lodge that he no
longer believed in God and that he no longer believed in the tenets of
Freemasonr y. The accused was duly served and did not answer. The
letter to the Secretary is a part of the record and states:
"Please remove my name from the roster of Heritage Lodge No.
764 as I no longer believe in God or the tenets of Free Masonry"
The accused also repeated his statements to several brethren. The Master of the Lodge was appointed Trial Master and after investigation
found the accused guilty of both counts and of unmasonic conduct and
fixed the penalty at expulsion.
"Landmark Nineteenth' ' as expressed in "The Foundation of Masonic Law" authorized by this Grand Lodge to be published in the
appendix to the California Masonic Code is as follows:
"A belief in the existence of God as the Grand Architect of the
Universe."
This Grand Lodge has repeatedly held that while Masonry is not a
religious order, it requires a belief in the existence and omnipotence of
a Supreme Being as a qualifkation for membership. ( 1857 Proc. p. 105;
1894 Proc. pp. 541, 771; 1900 Proc. pp. 644, 902). And also that making
a public or even a private declaration that one does not believe in God
is a Masonic offense for which charges should be preferred a nd, if found
guilty, the accused should be expelled. This Grand Lodge has also held
that no Brother will be permitted to resign from Masonry or renounce
the Order. He may withdraw from a particular Lodge of which he is a
member, but to renounce Masonry is an offense and should be punished.
( 1900 Proc. pp. 641, 899.)

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

83

We feel that this man has no place in Masonry and therefore offer
the following Resolution:
RESOLVE D . that the finding of guilt and the expulsion of the member of Heritage Lodge No. 764 are ratified, affirmed and approved.
Adopted.
TRIA L RECORD No. 1893
This case appears to fall squarely within the provisions of Section
733 C.M.C. and, in the opinion of your Committee, requires a reversal
of the purported expulsion and a trial of the accused.
The chronology of the proceedings is important and must be followed
closely.
On February 24 , 1965, accused was convicted of and sentenced for
the crime of manslaughte r.
On June 17, 1965, a notice was served on him, pursuant to Sec. 732
C.M.C. that a record of the conviction had been filed in the Lodge and
that, unless he demanded a trial within 60 days, he would be declared
expelled on September l , 1965. This date, September 1, will hereafter
be referred to as the noticed date.
On August 12, 1965, within 60 days of the notice . accused wrote the
Lodge demanding a trial. On August 14. charges were preferred by the
Junior Warden under Section 733 C.M.C.
The trial demand of the accused, dated August 12. is clearly a
dema nd for trial under Sec. 732 and was properly complied with by
the filing of the August t 4 charges.
Under existing Masonic law, a trial demand under Sec. 732 cannot
be withdrawn after the noticed da te: in this case. September 1, t 965.
See: C.M.C. Sec. 733b and Trial Record No. 1595. Proceedings of
Grand Lodge, 1958, p. 277.
On September t 6, 1965. accused fi led a written withdrawal of his
demand for trial.
In the opinion of your Committee this withdrawal was ineffective and
impermissible, and all proceedings thereafter taken, including the purported expulsion of the accused, are void and of no effect until he has
had the trial as demanded.
In order to clarify the course of further proceedings . if ordered, your
Committee wishes to state that the trial referred to by it is the trial of
the charges preferred on August t 4, 1965, which charges comply with
Sec. 733, C .M.C.
We offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D. that the purported expulsion of Charles Adams Johns
by Mt. Jackson Lodge No. 295 is reversed and set aside and the Lodge
is directed to proceed against him as provided in the California Masonic
Code.
Adopted.
