TRIAL RE~ORD No. I 899
A member of Walana Lodge No. 13 of the Philippines was expelled
by that Lodge on March 20, I 963. He was also a member of Lebanon
Lodge No. 495.
Section 432, subsection 6, of the California Masonic Code provides
that expulsion of a plural member in one Lodge immedia tely terminates
his membership in all Lodges.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution :
RESOLVED: That the member of Walana Lodge No. 13, expelled
by tha t Lodge, be declared expelled from Lebanon Lodge No. 495 as of
March 20. 1963.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1900
A member of Koolau Lodge No. 801 was charged with making a
false statement to the investigating committee in that he alleged he was
married, when in fact he was living with a woman to whom he was not
married. He was further charged with becoming involved in a domestic
controversy with her, whereupon she separated from him disclosing he
was never married and had two illegitimate children.
The accused plead not guilty in the Lodge. A trial by a commission
was had and he was found not guilty. Your Committee has found, however, that the trial record indicates that one o f the witnesses and the
accused were not sworn as Mas ter Masons.
We therefore offer the following resolution :
RESOLVED: That the finding of not guilty in Trial Record No.
1900 be reversed and the matter be remanded for a new trial.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD No. 1901
. A member of San Gabriel Lodge No. 546 was charged giving fals ifying answers in his application for the degrees in Masonry in that he had
in fact been rejected by a Lodge previously a nd had been convicted of
a crime, both of which he ha d denied in his application.
Th e Trial Master made a finding that the accused did not request
an investigation w as had, the accused was found guilty, and
trial.
a
expelled. The record indica tes the accused mis takenly sent his plea of
not guilty and request for trial to the accuser, the Junior W a rden,
instead of the M as ter.
The Committee therefore feels tha t the a ccused should be allowed
the privilege of a trial.
We offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the finding of guilt and the expulsion of the
accused member in Trial Record 1901 be reversed and the matter remanded to San Gabriel Lodge No. 546 with directions to again notify
the accused and allow him the opportunity of a trial.
Adopted.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
To supervise and direct the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the
Inspectors in the performance of their duties, and to require conformity
with the adopted ritual and work is the first, and most certainly one of
the most encompassing duties ascribed to the Grand Lecturer. In essence, this annual report of the services of the Grand Lecturer is directed
toward the activities carried on in compliance of this pa rticular responsibility, and others. as prescribed in Section 156 of the California
Masonic Code.
During the year there were two changes in the personnel of the
Ritual Committee, 27 new Inspectors appointed to fill vacancies, with
several more having tentative approval for future appointment to existing inspectorships. This is indicative of the responsiveness of the members of the lnspectoral Corps to the recently adopted Committee tenure
policy.
At the dose of last year's Annual Communication, Worshipful

91

Arthur J. Kahn, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 3, announced his
decision to retire from service on the Ritual Committee after approximately 14 years of faithful service. Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith .
Grand Master, on my recommendation, appointed Worshipful William
F. Poynter, Past Master of Veritas-Jonathan No. 545, Inspector of the
336th District, San Francisco, to fill the vacancy. Then, early this year,
Worshipful W. Ben Sorrells, A ssistant Grand Lecturer, Division 6,
announced his desire to be relieved of his duties after 10 years of devoted
service. Upon my recommendation, the Grand Master appointed Willia m H. Price, Past Master of E vergreen No. 259, Inspector of the 616th
District, Riverside, to fill this vacancy. Brother P oynter and Brother
Price have amply demonstrated their abilities to carry on in the foo tsteps of their predecessors.
The turnover in the lnspectoral Corps remains at a constant level.
prompted by such factors as change of employment, departure from the
area served, illness, and consideration of the length of tenure. This
latter reason for resigning was best exemplified in the attitude of such
Brothers as Hubert Raymond and Samuel G. Clark, who acknowledged
the joy and satisfaction of serving through the years, and at the same
time expressing the desire to step aside to allow others the opportunity
to serve in the rewarding experience of Inspector in this jurisdiction.
Following the close of our Annual Communication a year ago, at
the request of our Grand Master, a period of instruction was conducted
by the Grand Lecturer to acquaint the new corps of officers with their
new duties and responsibilities, particularly with regard to the Special
Communication:; of the Grand Lodge and Gra nd Lodge Ceremonies.
The wisdom of such instruction is attested to by the positive and dignified
manner in which the various officers have performed their duties at the
various Communications and Ceremonies held during the year, and at
the opening of our A nn ual Communication this morning.
The Ritual Committee met in Sacramento November 26-28 for its
annual review and exemplification of the ritual and lectures, and the
consideration of matters pertaining to the duties and responsibilities of
the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the Inspetcors. Also, the Ritual Committee met during the course of each of the Annual D ivisional Inspectors'
Conferences to discuss matters pertinent to their duties.
During the Spring months. the Inspectors' Conferences were held
as follows :
Div!sions 1 and 2-at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 17-19, conducted by
Worshipful Clare B. Campbell, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division l,
and Worshipful Frank P. Lemen, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 2;
. ~ivision 3-at Santa Rosa, April 22-24, conducted by Worshipful
W1l11am F. Poynter, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 3;
Division 4-at Sonora, June 3-5, conducted by Worshipful Wallace
H. Fiske, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 4;

Division 5-at San Diego, May 13-15. conducted by Worshipful
Robert A. Crigler, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 5; and
Division 6-at Long Beach, March 25-27, conducted by Worshipful
W. Ben Sorrells, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division 6.
The Conferences were made more meaningful to the Inspectors by
the presence of Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith, Grand Master.
Right Worshipful Laurence E. Dayton, Deputy Grand Master, Right
Worshipful John F. Porter, Senior Grand Warden, Right Worshipful
Eugene S. Hopp. Junior Grand Warden, and Most Worshipful Edward
H. Siems, Past Grand Master and Grand Secretary. At each conference,
the brethren were inspired by the remarks fitting to the occasion by our
Grand Master as he addressed each group in turn. They were further
encouraged by the thoughts expressed for the future by our Deputy
Grand Master as he projected his thoughts for the year ahead.
The most recent meeting for the purpose of instruction in the Ritual
and lectures was held last Saturday. October 8th. and is designated in
our Code as the Grand Lecturer's Lodge of Instruction for Inspectors.
to be held at the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. This
session was attended by the entire Ritual Committee and approximately
180 Inspectors. Representative Inspectors from the various Divisions
participated in the presentation of all the ritualistic work and lectures
of the three degrees.
In addition to the foregoing periods of instruction, each Assistant
Grand Lecturer has conducted a regular schedule of Schools of Instruc~
tion for the Inspectors within his Division, covering in addition to the
Ritual and Lectures. such other subjects as balloting, investigations,
reception of the flag. promotion of Grand Lodge committee programs.
and related matters pertinent to the welfare of the Craft.
It is gratifying to observe that the caliber of work presented by the
Inspectors at the Spring Conferences and at the School of Instruction
held last Saturday indicates another positive step forward toward our
ultimate goal of achieving complete uniformity in the work throughout
the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California. The Inspectors cannot be commended too highly for their sincere attention to detail and
their obvious desire to strive for perfection in this great responsibility.
The annual reports of the Inspectors are a further indication of the
tremendous service being rendered throughout our many Masonic Districts of the jurisdiction by this hard working. devoted, and dedicated
group of brothers. Their reports indicate a trend toward consistent
instruction and counselling with the Lodges, and increasing participation in programs and activities within the Lodges of the Districts. Their
reports also indicate instances of problems and difficulties in some
Lodges, and a concern and determination on the part of the Inspector
to assist in whatever manner possible to solve these problems.
May I pause here to acknowledge the fine, unseIBsh and continuous

service rendered by the Inspectors during the year, and to express to
them my deepest thanks for their devoted and conscientious efforts at
the "grass roots" level in behalf of Masonry in general and our Grand
Lodge in particular.
During March of this year. the Grand Lecturer vi£ited and consulted
with the officers of the Lodges of Hawaii. conducted the annual School
of Instruction for the Inspectors and Officers' Coaches of the various
Lodges. and conducted a special School for Candidate Coaches in
Honolulu. It is gratifying to observe, and to assure you, the continuing
improvement in the work in our sister state. It is testimony to the
conscientious and devoted service of our three Inspectors on the isla nds.
the Officers' Coaches who give so unstintedly of their time. and the
Brethren and officers of the Lodges who carry forth the torch of Masonry in this very important segment of our jurisdiction. Their hospitality
is warm. generous. and. I might add, sometimes overwhelming.
During the year it w as my privilege to visit the jurisdictions of
Nevada, Texas, and Louisiana, and to learn something of their varied
systems of control over the Ritual and the teaching of the work. During
the Annual Communication s of the Grand Lodge of Nevada. at Reno.
and the Grand Lodge of Texas, at Waco, opportunity was afforded to
consult and compare practices and procedures with our counterparts in
those jurisdictions; and in Louisiana. in company with our Grand Master.
Myron E. Smith. much information and printed material was obtained
from their genial Grand Secretary, D. Peter Laguens, Jr.
The program for the education of our Candida tes through the Candidate Coaches' Handbook program, as indicated by the Inspectors' annual
reports, continues to increase in favor and implementation . This program .
which we feel is vital to the growth and progress of our Fraternity. will
continue to demand our attention to achieve greater effectiveness in this
area of our endeavors. We ask that the Masters and Wardens of our
Lodges share this concern and determination with us.
Our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith, has displayed an earnestness in all things Masonic, and in sharing with him
this phase of responsibility to our Grand Lodge, we express to him our
sincere thanks for his great concerns for the success of our activities, and
his ready helpfulness in promoting the principles, ideals, and progress of
our great order.
We have found our Grand Secretary. Most Worshipful Edward H.
Siems. to be most helpful. as in the past. in various capacities during the
year. He and his staff have been most helpful in keeping our procedures
and communication s on schedule. and again merit our appreciative
thanks.
In closing, your Grand Lecturer is happy to assure you that this
past year has afforded ample evidence of the continual uphill course
toward the achievement of the goals of this office-Confor mity to our

Referred to Committee on Finance.

At the beginning of the year, the Board decided to meet monthly as
a whole Board, alternating from north and south and at such times most
convenient to the line officers. Heretofore, full Board meetings were
held quarterly with the north and south trustees meeting separately every
other week in the north and in the south to expedite the work of the
Board. The plan employed this last year seems to have bound the Board
together as a working Board and consequently more adequately performed the Board's functions.

U NION CITY

This past year has been an eventful as well as successful year in
many ways. The res idents that were receiving nursing care on the fourth
floor of the Home. were transferred to the fifth floor of Adams Hall in
August 1965 to comply with welfare requirements as they were considered non-ambulatory. These residents have ad justed quite well to their
new quarters and appear to be very happy. Since inaugurated, the move
required by the State of California Department of Social Welfare, the
President and the Secretary of the Board appeared before their representatives and pointd out that many of the residents transferred to the
fifth floor could be supervised adequately and safely in other portions of
the building complex, relieving the Home of additional expense of n ursing care. The representatives of the Department of Social Welfare concurred and an effort is being made to house some of our cane patients
previously considered non-ambulatory in other sections of the Home.
We were also informed that the other floors of Adams Hall could be
considered for non-ambulatory people and that the Department would
authorize such with proper application. Such an application is now in
progress.
Beca use of a new hous ing development close by. it was necessary to
erect a 6' chain link fence on the southern boundary of the Home and
around our water s upply tanks, as we were experiencing problems of
trespassing and vandalism.
The roads around the p roperty were repaired and oiled at the beginning of the rainy season to prevent damage to the roadways and the
slopes.
The drilling of a success ful well in a water bearing strata below that
presently used, will supplement our present water supply. From the two
wells now in use, sufficient water for many years to come should result.
Due to a change of administrative personnel at Covina, it was necessary to send Brother Gail David, the Superintendent at Union City, to
Covina the end of December, to take over as Acting Superintendent until
a replacement for Superintendent could be found . During the interval of
Superintendent David's absence Brother Hugh Herring, Assistant Superintendent. was selected as Acting Superintendent. He successfully
performed in this capacity without any interruptions in the services
rendered by the Home.

PkOCEED INGS OP THE

Due to the salary demand s of the Registe red Nurses in the area,
which began after the end of our fiscal period, it was found necessa ry to
increase the salaries of our six Registe red Nurses . There was general
concurr ence that the salaries of the nurses were on the low side when
compar ed with the compen sation paid for similar professi onal services by
other institutions. This increase was made conditio nal based upon the
final settleme nt with the nurses in the area. The nurses' aides . maids, and
kitchen help also demand ed increases which were in line with the salaries
being paid in the local area and on this basis they were approve d. The
salary increase s may exceed $125,000 per year.
For a number of months the Board has been studyin g the impact of
M edicare upon the Home's operatio n. All but two of our guests at Union
City have enrolled under Medica re. The two not covered are below the
age of 65. At the August meeting of the Board, a contrac t for one year,
retroact ive to July I, 1966, was entered into with the Palo Alto Clinic on
a trial basis. This contrac t not only enlists the full aid and support of
the Clinic in medical and surgical problem s but also covers an area not
served by Medica re ref erred to as M edigap. The propose d contrac t does
not include some of the services previou sly received and an effort is being
made to adjust this condition. Change s may have to be made as the year
progres ses. All these matters are subject to the interpre tation by the
Federal Departm ent of Health. Educati on and Welfar e. Should some
of these conditio ns be conside red as not being within the legal limits of
Medica re, it may be necessa ry to work on a month to month basis until
things are clarified in Washin gton. We have been assured that all the
Clinic services will go on uninterr upted.
During the coming year there will be changes necessa ry in certain
equipm ent, particul arly in the kitchen and dining room, and the replacement of possibly a station wagon and truck.
The append ed Superin tendent 's report will give some idea of the
complexities of operatio ns with which he is charged .

On June 30, 1966, the hospital contained 107 patients, plus 28
patients in the Charles Albert Ada ms Hall, w hich is under the supervision of the hospital. A ll were considered permanent in the hospital.
except 5.
In compliance w ith State Welfare Department requirements, the
fifth floor of Adams Hall was opened for non-ambulator y residents. The
move was made on the third of August and included all those who
needed nursing care or required a cane.
The Palo Alto Medical C linic continues to render ex pert medical
care for our residents.
We are happy to state there has not been any change d uring the
year in our administrative personnel. During the time I was Acting
Superintenden t at Covina, Brother Hugh H erring, Assistant Superintendent. did an outstan ding job in taking over here in Union City.
Both Mrs. Dagger, our Matron, and Mrs. Farris, our Hospital Supervisor, were very cooperative during the past year and have fulfilled their
duties most efficiently.
It has been our pleasure during the past year to receive many distinguished Masons, their families and guests as visitors to the Home.
Our guest book s hows signatures of 3,991 visitors, which represented
il 2 Lodges in our jurisdiction and 25 Lodges of other jurisdictions as
well as 6 foreign countries. Many Lodges visited the Home, enjoyed
picnic lunches, and conferred various degrees in the Temple. W e would
like to express our thanks to the Lodges for their generous contributions
to our Christmas Fund. With these we were able to make it a very
Merry Christm~s for all our residents. Our thanks also to all the groups
and individuals for other contributions, including clothing, televisions,
radios. cookies and cakes. Also, for the many fine programs a nd movies
presented in our auditorium a nd a ll other gifts.
On August 21, 1965, we were pleased to have approximately 700
members of the Eastern Star for the annual visit and Jam & Jelly Day
of the East Bay Past Matrons Association. They also held their annual
reception at the Home for the Worthy Grand M atron. Our thanks
to all this group for the canned fruits and juices that were contributed.
On Wednesday, October 13, we had the honor of having approximately 1,450 Masons, the representatives of Grand Lodge, and their
wives visit the Home and enjoy a picnic lunch. T his is a day looked
forward to each year with much an ticipation, especia lly by all of the
residents.
Another of the outstanding days of the year was the annual meeting
of the Most Worshipful M yro n E. Smith, Grand Master, and the Board
of Trustees on Jan uary 8, 1966. In the evening a reception was given for
the Grand Master at which time he gave us a very inspirational talk.
After the talk the residents had an opportunity to greet him and the
Trustees.

Our residents, during the year, enjoyed rides around the countryside in our 12 passenger bus. Larger buses were chartered for trips
to the ball game and ice follies.
During the past year a well was drilled on the property which is
now working and giving approximately 175 gallons per minute. This
is from a lower water bearing strata of water and is to supplement our
other well.
We found it necessary to install a six foot chain link fence, topped
with two strands of barbed wire, along part of the southern boundary
and around our water supply tank. This was necessary because we
had experienced an increasing problem of trespassing and vandalism.
It was also necessary to have our roadways repaired prior to the
winter rains.
On behalf of the staff, I wish to express our appreciation to all the
residents for their fine spirit and cooperation during the year.
To all the employees, my personal thanks to each of you for your
cooperation and assistance in caring for our residents.
To each of the Trustees, my personal thanks for your counseling
and continued confidence. Above all. our thanks to the Masons of California and Hawaii whose contributions and support make this rewarding
work possible. It is a sincere privilege and pleasure to serve both the
Trustees and the Fraternity as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for
the Aged.
Respectfully submitted,
GAIL H. DAVID, Superintendent

with a minimum of insecurity and tension , and the same can be said for
the staff. The interest, dedication and support of the Board of Trustees
and the Fraternity have helped make this transition more readily acceptable on behalf of all those concerned.
Our children have been involved in many and varied supervised
activities. Week-end and residential camping at Big Bear and a t the
beach have been enjoyed. Special trips to cultural and fine arts exh ibits
in the: local community have been arranged, as well as participation in
Masonic affiliated organizations, such as DeMolay, Job's Daughters,
Rainbow Girls. Serving as hosts and hostesses to groups on V isitation
Sunday, developing skills in music, dancing , participating on athletic
teams for the boys and friend ly competition with other Homes , have also
proven to be extremely meaningful in the lives of our children.
For the most part, our Home Family has enjoyed good health. A few
minor accidents have taken place but we have not suffered any serious
illnesses. We have continued the yearly physical examinations which
have included eye and dental exams. As a result of these in- depth physi~
cals we have been able to supply eye glasses for some children and
orthodontia for others. We are extremely grateful for the dedicated staff
of Magan Clinic, who have cared for our health needs.
An Alumni Committee of eight couples has been contacted and is in
process of organizing an "Alumni Association." It has made plans to con~
tinue the Annual Alumni Picnic in Covina to be held October 23rd this
year, and the Committee is also helping to plan "District Al umni
Events.'' One such event will be a dinner held in San Francisco early in
October. We a re.grateful to these alumni for their interest and efforts.
The coming year will see several things taking place-a fresh coat
of paint on all our buildings, an increased participation of our children
in the planning aspect of the Home activities on the part of selected staff,
and an intensification of an in-service training program for all s taff. We
will renew our dedication to meet the needs of the children in our Home
Family.
Please accept my s incere thanks for the many acts of kindness and
consideration shown me since May I st. Special thanks to the Board of
Trustees and the Masons in California and Hawaii whose interests and
efforts make possible our M asonic Home for Children .

REPORT OF THE SUPERINTENDENT-COVINA HOME
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is with pleasure that I submit my first Annual Report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children for the year ending June 30,
1966. The year's end showed a population of fifty-eight children in the
Home. Of these, thirty-four are boys and twenty-two are girls. In the
very near future our population will increase by three, two new boys
and one boy returned from leave of absence, making our Home Family
consist of sixty-one children.
Among the Charter O ak High School graduates in June, 1966,
Masonic Home contributed five---one young lady and four young men.
Of these five, the young lady is in business school as a result of a Masonic Homes Scholarship, one of the young men will be attending college
in September on another Homes Scholarship, one young man has enlisted in the armed services, the other two young men have secured employment and rejoined their families.
Our children seem to have accepted the change of administration

Respectfully submitted,
JAMES C. BLAIN E , Superintende nt

I NDIVIDUAL CONTRIBUTIONS THROUGH LODGES
Individual contributions this year amounted to $904,437.59-up from
$846,895.00 a year ago - contributed by 125,272 brethren, averaging
$7.22 per contributor - up from $6.84 a year ago. Many brethren, of
course, contributed in amounts of $100 to $500 and one brother gave
$10,000.00 through Dimond Lodge No. 603. His name is brother Horace
O. Lanza, a charter member of Dimond Lodge. Brother Lanza deserves
our special thanks for this unusually large contribution.
The over-all average contribution per member in all Lodges combined
was $3.71 compared to $3.46 per member a year ago.

Grand Lodge was called on at 9:30 a.m. the Grand Master presiding.

Mendocino Lodge No. 179. The invocation was delivered by the Grand
Chaplain. The minutes of the morning and afternoon sessions of Monday, October 10, were read and approved.

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
The M asonic Homes Endowment Board hereby s ubmits its Annual
Report for the fiscal year of July 1, 1965 through June 30, 1966.
INCOME FROM THE ENDOWMENT FUND
The in come from the Homes Endowment Fund this year was
$668,834.00 and that amount has been transferred to the operating expense account of our Masonic Homes. This is an increase of $69.441.00
above a year ago. If we did not have the Endowment Fund, that amount
of $668,834.00 would have had to have been raised by an additional
$2.75 in per capita tax.
BEQUESTS
Bequests in the amount of $203,335.00 were received into the Endowment Fund during the past year. In addition, $1.099.009.00 in bequests
were received by the Homes direct, from estates wherein the Endowment
Fund was not specifically mentioned in the Will. Thus a total of $1.302,344.00 was received from bequests during the fiscal year, hence the
importance of bequests.
The Endowment Board has consistently publicized the subject of
bequests, but has remained impartial as to whether the Endowment Fund
should be specified in the Will, or whether the bequest should be directed
to the Masonic Homes to be used at the discretion of the Board of Trustees. About 12 years ago this Board sent a letter and bequest folder to
several thousand attorneys, whether or not the attorneys were Masons.
In recent years we have concentrated our efforts upon getting bequest
material into the hands of attorneys w hom we know to be Masons. and
into the hands of individual M asons and their families.
During the past few years, this Board has furnished to the Lodges,
for sending to members. more than 700.000 folders dealing solely with
the subject of bequests. During the past year the Lodges have ordered
from this Board 113.000 of the current bequest folder, entitled "Masonic
Foot Prints," for sending to members. In addition, during the past three
years, the Chairman has sent five separate mailings of bequest material
to a list of I 700 attorneys whom we know to be Masons. All Lodges are
urged to continue to publicize to their members, the subject of bequests.

This year the Lodges ordered 1,771.818 printed items from the
Endowment Board for sending to members to publicize the Ho mes and
the Endowment and to promote greater contributions from the brethren.
This number includes 725,195 of the new two-color folders re contributions; 113,164 folders promoting bequests; 319,629 new two-color cards
and leaflets; 222,179 copies of the Grand Master's Proclamation concerning Endowment Month, with coupon attached; 212 ,413 combination
"dues and contribution" envelopes; and 179,238 Contribution Re minder
envelopes. Most of the Endowment Board budget is used in the printing
and distribution of the printed items.

Lorenza H. Shaw
Raymond C. Reeder
We give special recognition and thanks to the above Inspectors because when all Lodges in a District have an unusually high record for
the Endowment we have reason to believe that the Inspector of that
District has been especially enthusiastic and influential concerning the
Homes Endowment program of his Lodges. However, many other Inspectors may have been equally enthusiastic about the Endowment program as the above Inspectors but were kept off of the special list by one
Lodge. Those Inspectors also deserve our special thanks and recognition.

A year ago four Board Members resigned for health, business or personal reasons and were replaced as follows: M. Richard Andrews. Santa
Barbara. was appointed to replace Ralph C. Hine; John L. Taylor,
Santa Ana, was appointed to replace W .W. Reyburn; Robert L. Wing
was appointed to replace C. Raymond Winterhalder in the San Jose
area; and Robert D. Lintner, San Francisco, was appointed to replace
William M. Connor.
For the coming year the following Board Members whose term expires
in October, 1966, have requested that they not be re-appointed: John
L. Taylor, after serving for one year; George Q. Evans, after serving
for two years; Charles F. Minetti. after serving for 6 years; and Kermit
A. Jacobson, after serving for 12 years. the past nine years of which he
has been a devoted and efficient Vice Chairman of the Boa rd and has
been tremendously cooperative a nd helpful to the Chairman in particular
and to the Board and Masonry in general.
In addition to the above Members of the Board, Chairman John M .
Gordon announced a year ago his decision to retire from the Chairmanship after 1966. He has been a Member of the Board for 16 years and
Chairman for the past 9 years. He has now resigned as a Member of
the Board effective October 14, 1966.
During the past nine years, the position of Chairman has become
virtually a full-time job for nine or ten months a year, without compensation and without paid secretarial help. If it had not been for the constant and devoted assistance of his wife, Margaret. it would have been
necessary to spend a considerable amount of the Endowment Board
budget for secretarial service. It has been a " labor of love" for the
Chairman and his devoted wife.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

IN CONCLUSION

MEMORIALS

It is obviously impossible to give due and adequate credit and thanks
to all who have participated in the Homes Endowment Program during
the past yea r. They are legion - the Grand Lodge Officers and Past
Grand Masters; the Grand Lodge Committeemen; Grand Secretary and
his staff; the Grand Lecturer and his Assistant Grand Lecturers; the
Inspectors; Masters and Wardens; Lodge Secretaries and Endowment
committeemen of the Lodges; and last but certainly not least, the more
than 125.000 brethren and their families who contributed more than
$900.000.00 in contributions. and those who ha ve passed on to their
reward but who left Masonic Foot-Prints in the form of a bequest to
our Masonic Homes.
To all who participated by contributing time, effort, and/or cash
contributions, we extend our heartfelt thanks and appreciation, and pray
that their Masonic Foot-Prints may be firmly imprinted in the sands of
time.
Respectfully submitted,
THE MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
JoHN M. GORDON, Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON RETIREMENT PLAN
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In 1954, the Retirement Pension Plan was inaugurated for the employees of the Masonic Homes of California , the Grand Lodge of California and affiliates, to provide a retirement life income for employees
in addition to Social Security benefits, upon attaining the age of sixtyfive (65).
The plan had certain requirements to be eligible for membership. The
employee must have been in our employ for a period of two years and
attained the age of thirty ( 30) years.
In 1964, the original plan was amended to change conditions for
early retirement from age fifty-five ( 55) plus twenty ( 20 ) years of
service to age fifty-five ( 55) and fifteen ( 15) years of service.
As of December 31, 1965, the auditors report indicated total accrued
assets for both Masonic Homes and Grand Lodge and componen t
organizations of $824 .074. up from $744,210 last year. Of the total.
$505.383 is attribu table to Masonic Homes and $318,691 is attributable
to the Grand Lodge and component organizations.
Since August 8, 1966 the Plan has been improved to recalculate
pension credits for all service to D ecember 31. 1965, based on the average salary in the period from January 1, 1961 to December 31. 1965 .
When the Plan was ins talled 11 years ago, the benefit for service
prior to the effective date of the Plan was based on the salary a s of the
effective date and was 1Yi7o of s uch salary for each year of credited
service prior to t,he effective date. For credited service after the effective
date, pension credits are based on 2 % of the covered salary earned in
each year. The recompu tation of credits to December 31. 1965, has been
based on the same 1Yz % for each year of prior service and 2 % for each
year of current service, but has been applied to the average salary in
the years 1961 through 1965.
The effect of the recomputation is to increase the accrued credits for
those employees who have more than five years of credited service. Also
for those employees who will retire in the near fu ture, the recomputation
will put their pensions largely on a final salary basis rather than on
career average salary.
Consideration has also been given to bringing our present Retirement Plan more nearly in line with pension plans currently being adopted by allowing employees pension credits for the two ( 2) year w aiting
period. It is pointed out that the current two yea r waiting period would
be required, but once the employee established employment beyond that
point and reaches the age of retirement, he would receive pension credits fro m the original da te of employment.
The Committee also took under consideration the one employee currently under the plan w ho was employed prior to reaching the age

REPORT OF THE TRUSTEES
CALIFORNI A MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This is the Twelfth Annual Report of the Board of Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple.
At the close of the 1965 Annual Communicatio n of Grand Lodge
the Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple met in Annual
Meeting. The President. Ralph H. Head, reported the election of
Laurence E . Dayton as Deputy Grand Master, John F. Porter as Senior
Grand Warden, and Eugene S. Hopp as Junior Grand Warden. On
proper motion they were duly elected members of the Board of Trustees
as provided in the California Masonic Code.
The Board then proceeded to organize with Ralph H. Head as
President, Samuel I. Jacobs as Vice-President , Paul A . Pflueger, Grand
Treasurer, as Treasurer, and Edward H. Siems, Past Grand Master and
Grand Secretary. as Secretary.
The terms of the appointed members of the Board were as follows:
Expiring in 1966, T. Galt Atwood and Chester R. MacPhee; expiring in
1967, Samuel I. Jacobs and Howard H. McKinley; and expiring in 1968
Lyle Patton and Ralph H. Head.
It was revealed by an economist a short time ago that during the
next forty years we will build in this country a second America. By the
year 2000 our population will have increased to more than 340,000.000
and in order to provide for this tremendous growth we must build
64,000,000 new homes and that is as many homes as we have built in
the United States from the time the Constitution was signed up until
the present time.
During the past ten years this Grand Lodge has laid the cornerstone,
has built, and has paid for the most beautiful and useful Grand Lodge
Masonic Temple in the United States.
We can now pause and ask ourselves the question. "Are we prepared to equip the occupants of these structures erected and yet to be
constructed with certain built-in truths and principles which must be
possessed by the majority if our great heritage of freedom is to be passed
on?"

The incident pointed up to the Trustees the need for the formulation of a complete and comprehensive rent and leasing policy for the
auditorium and exhibit hall. On August 5, 1966. the Trustees adopted
a policy which not only reiterated but clarified the prohibition of the
use of the facilities for merchandising, including the sale on the premises
of any kind of merchandise whether at retail or wholesale. The display
of goods by industrial firms and business associations for exhibit purposes only was permitted. However, a prohibition was added against
meetings of political parties. organizations, and action groups.
Within the structure of the Board of Trustees a Committee on
rentals consisting of three Trustees was appointed to examine the
proposed use of the facilities and to give approval when all requirements
have been met.

To the Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple:
Brethren :
The burning of the Temple mortgage, at the Annual Communication
of Grand Lodge this year is heartwarming news for all California and
Hawaii Masons.
After eight years of use this magnificent and stately edifice continues
to be widely accepted as a major cultural center.
TOURS ANO VISITATIONS
Our Temple is open for visitors Monday through Friday. from 8:45
A .M. to 4 :45 P .M .. and we maintain visiting hours on Saturdays and
Sundays, from 12 :00 Noon to 4 :00 P .M. This has enabled many of our
brethren and visitors from other areas to see the Temple. During the
last year more than 3,500 visitors from many lands have signed our
register, and thousands more have come to see and admire. It is an
interesting experience to welcome these visiting brethren and dignitaries,
who are impressed with the unusual beauty and dignity of our facilities.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
At the 1965 Communication of Grand Lodge the dispensation of
Gateway Lodge U.D. was continued for the succeeding year. Boron
Lodge U.D. was instituted on November 27, 1965, and Maccabee Lodge
U .D. was instituted on December 15, 1965. All three Lodges have petitioned for charters.
Each of the Lodges has submitted its records for examination and
representatives, accompanied by their Inspectors, have appeared before
the Committee.
The Committee found that in each case the requirements necessary
to qualify for a charter have been met and the records submitted were
satisfactory.
Gateway Lodge U . D., located in the City of Seaside. is especiatly
commended for the progress they have made during the past year under
dispensation. The additional year has enabled them to solve many of
their problems and we believe that this Lodge will be a definite asset to
Masonry in its area.
Boron Lodge U . D ., located in the tow n of Boron on the Mojave
Desert, deserves special mention. This aggressive group of Masons has
constructed a temple which will be deeded to the Lodge free of debt as
soon as the Lodge is constituted.
Maccabee Lodge U.D., located in the City of Rosemead, submitted

THE GEORGE WASHINGTON
MASONIC NATIONAL MEMORIAL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
It is a pleasure for me to report briefly on the fifty-fifth annual meeting of the George Washington M asonic National Memorial Association
held at the Memorial in Alexandria. Virginia on February 22, 1966.
It was a s:ireat honor for me when I was elected in February, 1962 to
fill the unexpired term of Past Grand Master Lloyd E. Wilson as a
director of the Association. A subsequent term of three years ended this
year and I am pleased to report tha t I was re-elected to serve as a director of the Association for another three-year term, to expire in February,
1969.
My pleasure arises out of this recognition, not to me, but to the
Masons comprising the Grand Lodge of California who have supported
the Memorial from its inception. You will recall from previous reports
that Past Grand Master Oscar Lawler was prominent in the initial
proceedings to establish the Memorial. Other Grand Masters of our
jurisdiction have served as State Representative in developing the financing of the Memorial, and then there was the monumental service
rendered by Lloyd Wilson as a Director and Member of the Executive
Committee of the Memorial Association.

143

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

Again I say that the Grand Lodge of California, and its members.
feel a deep interest in the Memorial and what it represents, even thoug h
we a re separated from it by several thousand miles.
First, I would like to comment briefly on the Conference of Grand
Masters of Masons in N orth America which is held annually in conjunction w ith the meeting of the Memorial Association.
California was represented so ably by its Grand Master. Myron E.
Smith; by its Deputy Grand Master, Laurence E. Day ton; and by its
Grand Secretary. Edward H. Siems. These brothers played an important
part in the Conferences of Grand Masters and Grand Secretaries. Past
Grand Master Henry C. Clausen was also present as nn officer of the
Supreme Council of the Southern Jurisdiction of the Scottish Rite, and
he saw to it that his fellow Californians were received and welcomed
most heartily at the House of the Temple when those attending the
Conference were guests o f the Supreme Council at a luncheon.
Modesty on the part of the Grand M aster and the Deputy Grand
Master will probably preclude their mentioning that they were received
into practice before the Supreme Court of the United States by the Chief
Justice, Earl Warren, Past Grand Master of this Jurisdiction.
To return to the meeting of the Memorial Association, we convened
at 10:00 A .M . on February 22, 1966 in the Memoria l Building on
Shooters Hill in Alexandria in the presence of those in attendance at
the Grand Masters Conference, together with representatives from concordant and other Masonic Bodies and from numerous M asonic Grand
Lodges from without the boundaries of North America.
From the facts contained in the annual reports which were presented
at the meeting, it is good to be able to report progress, even if not
substantial, in the operations of the Memorial. The Endowment Fund
grows slowly and the funds, invested like ours here in California, are
administered in a wise and prudent manner. Contributions to the operating and maintenance fund have enabled the Board of Directors to step
up maintenance of the property and to begin work on long deferred improvements.
Brethren, in this Memorial you have an asset of much physical value
but a much greater value is that of an intangible nature-a value which
reaches into the hearts and minds of all who come to its doors -for,
surely, inspiration to the heart and mind lies within its portals.
It is inspirational to view the Memorial and its exhibits. It is inspirational to be at the Memorial on the occasion of the annual meeting
and to be in the presence of the Masonic leaders of North America and
of other countries. Mos t of all, though, is to be in the presence of the
spirit of the one to whom the Memorial is dedicated, a brother who attended his Lodge in Alexandria a nd who sat as its first Master, even
while serving as the first President of his country. And there is the
inspiration to be gained from the visit to the home of George W ashing-

ton at nearby Mt. V ernon and to his final resting place there on the
banks of the P otomac. This visit, or pilgrimage, concludes each annual
meeting of the Memoria l Association.
Th.is year, a dream was realized in the dedication of the George
Washington Museum which now occupies the fourth floor of the Memorial. W e are indebted to the Northern and Southern Jurisdictions of
the Supreme Councils of the Scottish Rite for the fu nds which made the
museum a reality.
At the dedication ceremony, special guests included the Sovereign
Grand Commanders of the two Scottish Rite Jurisdictions, the Misses
A~ne and Patty Washington , who contributed valuable family memorabilia to the museum and Sena tor E verett Dirksen, 33rd Degree Mason,
who gave the Dedicatory Address. The Memorial was also presented
with one of the foundation stones removed from the White House when
it was restored and remodelled during Brother H arry Truman's Presidency of the United States. It was noticed by Brother Truman that the
foundation stones which were being removed from the White H ouse
bore the markings of a Master Mason, so he had a sufficient number of
s tones laid aside in order to present one to each Grand Lodge in the
United States.
So, my brethren, I remind you again-this is your Memorial. Visi t it
if you can for you will find the effort most worthwhile.
How important it is that the Masons of this country have a national
memorial or s hrine which attracts people of every race and creed . How
i~p?rta~t. it is that all M<tsons know about it and have a par t in maintammg 1t m a manner creditable to the fraternity.
Particularly ls this memorial most important to all Masons whithersoever dispersed, bearing, as it does , the name of the first citizen of the
land, our distinguished brother, George Washington, Mas ter Mason.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON COMMERCIALISM

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
The Committee on Distribution, to which has been referred the Annual Message of the Grand Master and the reports of the Grand Treasurer, the Grand Secretary. the Grand Lecturer and the Trustees of the
Masonic Homes. submits the following report:

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism herewith submits its report for
the year just ending.
There have been no infractions of our laws, rules and regulations
requiring serious action on the part of this Committee. There have been
several matters, which from their nature, were of necessity referred to
our Most Worship£ ul Grand Master for his determination.
Our symbolic Lodges have presented no insurmountable problems
nor have the concordant Scottish and York Rite Bodies.
It is the appendant prerequisite organizations which have necessitated a good portion of our Committee's work. Additionally there were
a few individual members of the craft plus the profane which required
the balance of our investigations.
Generally speaking the Shrine Temples have been most cooperative,
a number of them have asked for guidance in arranging prospective
events some of which were restricted to Masonic groups and others
open to the general public such as football games. boxing tournaments.
et cetera.
One temple arranged several f!WUp travel tours for its memberstravel brochures and other material to be mailed to its membership were
submitted to the Committee for clearnnce in order to make sure that the
matter contained there was not in violation, in all instances suggested
changes were observed.
There were some matters in regard to the Imperial Shrine Session
recently held in. San Francisco which have been referred to our Grand
Master for bis determination.
A Shrine Club in a populous section of the State advertised in the
local newspaper "A 5th Annual Luau" to be held in a public restaurant,
no reservation needed. 21 or over welcome, driving directions, etc. No
mention was made of the recipient charity. When called to the attention
of the Potentate under which the Club operated, a meeting of the Divan
was promptly convened and the President of the Club was removed
from office for having violated Masonic and Shrine law relative to
advertising.
Fund raising proposals of certain appendant groups, such as bazaars
and other schemes were submitted for clearance; unfortunately, in most
instances they were contrary to Grand Lodge regulations which were
pointed out to the inquiring person.
We have again had called to our attention several instances of the
mis-use of the Masonic symbol (the Square and Compass). Our investigation developed in most situations that the offending persons were
members of organizations not recognized by this Grand Lodge. The
attention of the offenders has been called to the fact that our symbols

We recommend that the portions of the Grand Secretary's Report
herein listed be referred to the committees indicated:

2. That portion relating to Lodge consolidations to the Committee

Homes have gone direct to the Committee on Finance so no action by us
is necessary.
We have carefully read and reviewed the Grand Master's inspiring
message. We congratulate him on the brevity and clarity of the message.
We join with all the Masons of California in extending grateful appreciation for the dedication and devotion he has given to the Grand
Lodge during this Masonic Year.

are the property of this Grand Lodge and, as such, registered under the
Corporation Code of the State of California and that unauthorized use
is subject to cease and desist under the law. In practica lly all instances
assurance was given that unlawful use would be discontinued. We had
called to our atten tion two instances where Masters had personal cards
carrying the square and compass. the Lodge name and number, together
with their home and bus iness phones and also business and residence
addresses. This practice is not general so far as we could learn. Additionally, we found that a Past Master continued to use the card after he
had completed his term of office; the individual was contacted, he agreed
to discontinue the practice and to destroy remaining cards.
Your Committee has had referred to it by a number of prerequisite
organizations questions relating to fund raising projects such as bazaars
and other schemes which could conflict with our regulations. In a ll such
matters the requirements and prohibition of our regulations were pointed
out and a copy of the regulations made available to the inquiring organizations. We have had no report of any violations.
We have recently had called to our attention the activity of a Chicago publishing concern in contacting the Order of Rainbow for girls
to sell cook books. This matter is being investigated and will be reported
on later.
A possible mis-use of the Grand Lodge roster was called to our
attention when several solicitation letters were addresed to a Grand
Lodge officer who had been active in Masonic Research. Our investigation ascertained that travel and convention bureaus throughout the
State keep a list of such activities including the name of the person to
be contacted for use in endeavoring to bring the group to their area for
meetings. Tha t no Grand Lodge roster was used was evident from our
investigation.
Your Committee does not initiate investigations. Our action starts
when complaints are received. usually through the Grand Lodge, though
occasionally from members. In all cases we endeavor to take corrective
action by whispering good counsel. This we feel is far better for peace
and harmony than to cause turmoil.
There were a number of other matters handled routinely but none
of sufficient importance to warrant special mention.
Your Committee appreciates and wishes to thank the helpful cooperation of all called upon-the Inspectors, the Gra nd Lodge officers,
but especially the Grand Secretary and the Grand Master who were
so generous with their time and so understanding of our problems. It
was a genuine pleasure to have worked under and with them.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its sixteenth year of ac tivity,
and herewith renders its report for the twelve mo~ths .ended June 30.
1966. Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical b~ckground
and basic information, which should be help ful to those attendmg Grand
Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent M an Rule in modified form was adopted by and for
Grand Lodge at the 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges
a Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California was formed for the purpose of administering the investable fun~s
of Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California, a nd the M asonic
Homes Endowment Fund.
The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constit~ent
Lodges, but Grand Lodge makes the services of its investment ~dv1sor
available to the Lodges without charge. Many Lodges are makmg use
of this service.

this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance

invested in any one Association shall not exceed the amount
covered by insurance.

sixty per cent (as the case may be) of the total market value of all the
cash, bank account s and securities held,"-the controlling point being
that there cannot be more than 20% or 60 % invested in Groups II and

The Grand Secretary, Edward H. Siems, P.G.M., acts as Secretary
of the Committee.
By Ordinance, under Section 246 (formerly 86) with respect to
investments of Grand Lodge funds, and Section 403 (formerly 152.l )
respecting investments by Constituent Lodges, the following provisions,
as briefed, prevailed as of June 30, 1966. (See Sections 246 and 403,
C.M.C.):
GROUP I. At least 20% of the funds available for investment must
be in:
A) Cash and/or bank accounts.
B) Obligations of the United States.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions.
D) Such other securities as are legal investments for savings
banks in California or Hawaii (as amended 1959).
GROUP II. Up to 20 % may be invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness. which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an exchange registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that this listing requirement shall not
apply to evidences of indebtedness of corporations whose
common stock is eligible for investment under the provisions
of Section III (a) hereof.
B) Preferred stocks, which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange.
except that this listing requirement shall not apply to pref erred stocks of corporations whose common stock is eligible
for investment under the provisions of Section III (A) hereof.

No such investments, however, shall be made which at the time of
purchase will result in the total market value of the securities referred
to in this section exceeding twenty per cent ( 20%) of the total market
value of all the cash. bank accounts and securities held. (As amended
1965).

I).
At the 1959 Communication certain amendments were passed with
respect to the percentages which could be invested in Groups I and III.
Group I was reduced to 20% and Group III was increased to 60%. In
this connection, it is very important to call attention to the followi ng,
which is contained in the Reports of the Committee on Jurisprudence
and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
"Your Committee on Jurisprudence respectfully calls atten tion to
the fact that this proposed amendment is permissive only and is not a
directive. Great care should be exercised in making investments under
the authority granted by this proposed amendment."
"Your Committee on Policy and General Purpose recommends the
adoption of Resolution D-7 but with this admonition to the Lodges :
"A) The authority granted is permissive only and is not suggested
as an investment guide under present e.c onomic conditions.
"B) That in making investments in Group III the Lodges be most
circumspect in taking advantage of this additional authority.
"C) And that they strictly comply with the provisions of the last
paragraph of Section 403 of our Ordinances, to consult with and heed
the advice of the professional investment advisors used by Grand Lodge,
and made available to the Constituent Lodges without charge to the individual Lodge."
The above comments are included in the reports of the Committees
as they appear on page 282 of the 1959 Proceedings.

At the 1960 Communication Section 403 was amended. as follows:
"The provisions of this section requiring securities to be fully listed
and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange, shall not apply
to the Honolulu Stock Exchange. This exception is confined to Lodges
located in the State of Hawaii." (The Honolulu Stock Exchange is not
as yet a National Securities Exchange, as defined by the Securities and
Exchange Commission).
We would also like to call your attention to the fact that there is a
circular issued by Grand Lodge regarding the investment of funds by
Constituent Lodges, which is available at the Grand Secretary's office.
Since its formation, the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. Between quarterly meetings the business of the
Committee is conducted by correspondence or telephone.

Endowment Fund contributions made through the Lodges amounted
to $904,438 for the year ended June 30, 1966. Other gifts and bequests
for the Endowment Fund amounted to $203,335 bequests, $36,067
memorials and $7,789 miscellaneous, or a total of $247.191. For the
General Fund gifts and bequests, and memorial contributions from individuals and organizations, amounted to $1,099,009, (which also includes real estate and items other than stocks and bonds). The Masonic
Homes Board of Trustees determines how these gifts and bequests are
allocated-such allocations a re made in accordance with specific bequests, or in the absence of such at the direction of the Trustees. The
Endowment Fund contributions remain in that Fund, and only the income is used.

the Crocker Citizens National Bank, at its One Montgomery Street Office, San Francisco.
We have had excellent attendance at our Investment Committee
meetings during this year, as has been the case since this Committee was
organized. We were very pleased to have M. W. Grand. Master Theodore Meriam and Deputy Grand Master Myron E. Smith at our August, 1965 meeting. Deputy Grand Master Laurence E . Dayton has
attended all of the meetings this past year.
Again we come to that portion of the Investment_Commi~tee report
when we try to summarize in few words the financial and investment
outlook as we see it.

154

PROCEED INGS OP THE

Drastic changes have occured in our economy since last year's Report. As shown by the figures, our approach has been decidedl y conservative . Our common stock portfolio as of June 30, 1966. was down
to 37,Yi% against an allowabl e of 60% .
We have also been enabled to take advantag e of the better interest
rates. Consequ ently, our net income percenta gewise has been greatly
increased .
When common stock purchase s again become more attractiv e, our
fixed income maturitie s are so spaced that we can readily take advantag e
of the opportun ities which may be made available . Greater caution has
been our endeavo r for the last few yeors; conseque ntly, we are prepared
for investme nt opportun ities as they may appear. Special mention should
be made of the fact that our primary consider ation in common stock investment is for growth in value over a period of years, if necessar y,
rather than intermed iate market price changes.
We began to adopt a very conserva tive approach in common stock
holdings at our February 1966 meeting -we reduced consider ably further at our May meeting, and by June 30, 1966 our common stock holdings were down to 37.4 % of our entire portfolio, vs. 49.95 % on June 30,
1965 and a high of 57.6% on June 30, 1963.
If the higher level of interest rates continue s for some time, we
should show a substant ial increase in net income. especiall y so inasmuch
as 55.1 % of our portfolio is now invested in Group I-the category
which is most susceptib le to the higher fixed income. No one can predict
how long the present high yields will continue , but we have fortified ourselves by investing substant ial sums in non-calla ble obligatio ns running
up to I 0 years in maturity and at prevailin g higher income rates.
We again repeat that our course of action can be quite different
from that of an individua l for a variety of reasons. This statemen t is
made so as not to unduly influence individua ls who read our recomme ndations for Grand Lodge agencies in their personal investme nt programs.

the members of the Investme nt Committ ee for their wholehe arted and

REPOR T OF COMM ITTEE ON LODGE FINAN CING
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It is the intent of this report. respectfu lly ~ubmitted for your approval ,
to indicate the activities of the Committ ee on Lodge Financin g during
the past year. A review of the report discloses continue d activity in the
construc tion, maintena nce , and operation of Masonic Temples throughout the jurisdiction. A further study reveals a definite improvement in
the administ ration of the business and financial affairs of Masonic
T emples. During the past year 297 Temple Associat ions have submitte d
to the Committ ee for its informat ion, study, and review a statemen t of
financial status as required by Section 200 of the Masonic Code. These
reports reflect a definite and continuin g progress in Masonic Temple
fiscal processe s and controls. All of this has resulted in increased interest
in the financial affairs of the Lodges througho ut the jurisdicti on and
further indicates that they are being managed in a most efficient manner, and in almost every instance are being maintain ed in a state of
solvency. Each year more and more Lodges and Temple Associat ions
are establish ing .necessa ry cash and depreciat ion reserves, which are
so importan t for the repair, rehabilit ation. and replacem ent of the Temples as may be required in the future.
In the past year the Committ ee acted upon 79 applications relating
to the purchase of property , construc tion, maintena nce, and other matters concerni ng the financial operation of their Lodge facilities. The
Committ ee approved 18 applicati ons for the transfer of funds from the
Lodges to the Temple Associat ions for use in matters relating to Temple
construc tion, operation , and maintena nce; 11 requests for the purchase
of property for future Temple sites; five requests to enter into contracts
for the construc tion of new Masonic Temples ; 10 requests for capital
improvem ents, expansio n, renova ting, and repairs; eight requests to borrow funds; six requests to form Masonic Temple Associat ions for the
purpose of conducting the financial affairs of the Lodges; three requests
to enter into satisfact ory leasing agreeme nts ; I 0 requests to invest in
Temple Associat ion stock and other various items. This, together with
other miscellaneous items, required action of the Committ ee in more
than 120 proceedi ngs. Approxi mately 80 visitation s were made to
Lodges , at their request, to advise and counsel with the brethren concerning problems respectin g Lodge and Temple Associa tion matters .

156

157

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

These visitations were most successful and in all instances the problems
were resolved satisfactoril y to all concerned.
The Committee again points out the importance of keeping the
Masonic Temples in proper order and repair. A Masonic Temple in
disrepair reflects a very poor light in all of those who view it. A well
ordered Temple, both inside and out, gains the respect and regard of
the neighborhoo d and community in which it is located. So much can
be done with enthusiastic effort and little financing. The Committee
feels that it is the obligation of the Lodges to keep pace with the community in which they are a part. We urge you to continually view your
Temples in order to keep them and their surrounding s in such exemplary
condition that they will gain and hold the respect and support of the
community, which is so necessary for the success and growth of our
fraternity.
The Committee also recommends that Lodges and Temple Associations constantly review their insurance program in order that they may
be assured that they are properly covered in all requirement s necessary
to protect their property and their members. Also, that occasional review
be made as to their status relating to tax requirement s of local. state,
and federal agencies. The requirement s as to tax exemption should be
strictly adhered to in order that the individual Lodges, Temple Associations, and the fraternity conform to all existing laws relating to tax
matters.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To th e Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A M. of California:
Since filing our report for 1965, there have been changes in the
payroll tax laws which apply to our various Masonic organizations.
As has been our custom in past years, we present. for reference
purposes, the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the various
payroll taxes which will be in effect during the calendar year 1967 and
thereafter.
Now pending before the U. S. Congress is Bill H.R. 15119 (as
amended by the Senate Finance Committee) which would effect major
changes in both Federal and California Unemployment Tax, possibly
effective January 1, 1967, when the rate of Federal Unemployment Tax
would increase to .6% from the present .4%. The Federal taxable wage
base would be increased to $3,900.00 for 1968-1971 and $4,800.00

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

163

thereafter. The bill would also instigate changes for California purposes.
It is quite possible that this legislation will pass this year. Mention
thereof is made to post you on possible future developments.
FEDERAL WITHHOLDING (INCOME} TAX
All wages paid to employees of a Masonic Lodge are subject to
Federal income tax withholding. In order to determine the amount of
income tax which is to be withheld from wages paid to its employees.
the Lodge should ask each employee to complete and file with the Secretary of the Lodge a Federal Form W-4, "Employee's Withholding
Exemption Certificate." Reference to withholding tax tables furnished
by the Treasury Department will enable the Secretary to determine the
amount to be withheld.
As you know from the coverage accorded it in the press, there is a
definite possibility of a tax increase in 1967. In this event you would,
of course, have to secure new withholding tables.
FEDERAL INSURANCE CONTRIBUTIONS (SOCIAL SECURITY)
An employee of a Masonic Lodge is subject to tax for each calendar
quarter during which he earns $50, or more. The tax rates shown below
are applicable to the first $6,600.00 of wages paid to each employee
during the calendar year. These rates are to be paid by both the employer and the employee.

FEDERAL UNEMPLOYMENT TAX
Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if they employ four or
more individuals who are paid $50 or more per calendar quarter, pro~
viding they have first qualified as an "employer" by employing four or
more employees on at least one day in each of 20 or more weeks during
the calendar year, For this purpose, all paid employees of the Lodge,
including the Secretary and those who are performing ritualistic services
(Tiler. Organist, Soloist), should be counted if they receive $50 or more
per calendar quarter.

CALIFORNIA UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE TAX

Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if the total wages paid
during a calendar quarter to taxable employees are in excess of $100.
For this purpose a taxable employee is one who is paid $50 or more per
calendar quarter. However, whether or not elected or appointed officials
of a Lodge are to be counted as taxable employees will depend upon
whether or not the Lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax
Act.
If the Lodge is not subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act,
then the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be exempt
from California Unemployment Insurance Tax unless the wages paid
to these officials exceed $100 per month.
If the Lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, then
the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be subject to
California Unemployment Insurance Tax if the wages paid to these
officials amount to $50, or more, per calendar quarter.
For purposes of this tax, the term "elected or appointed official" will
include any official of the Lodge who is compensated for his services.
Those usually compensated for their services are the Secretary, Tiler,
Organist, and Soloist.
If the Lodge is subject to California Unemployment Insurance Ta~.
the tax rate shown below will be applicable to the first $3.800.00 paid
to each employee during the calendar year 1967. Only the employer
pays the tax . This base of $3,800.00 is effective for calendar year 19?7.
Thereafter it will fluctuate between $3,800.00 and $4.100.00 dependmg
upon the condition of the fund.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Public Schools has endeavored to carry forward
the ideas and programs of former committees and to initiate some inno~
vations and long range plans.
We have had the enthusiastic support and encouragement of the
Grand Master, Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith, and the other Grand
~dge line elective officers, as well as the Grand Secretary and his staff.
and to all of them we express our profound thanks.
The proclamation by the Grand Master announced the theme "Keep
America Strong ... Support Our Public Schools" and designated the
week of April 25-29, 1966 as Public Schools Week. Cooperation of
public and school officials throughout California and Hawaii resulted in
numerous supporting proclamations or pronouncements reaching to the
general public.
Among these was a Resolution passed by the Assembly of the Cali~
fornia State Legislature which, among other things , mentioned that
"Public Schools Week was created and sponsored by the Grand Lodge
of California, Free and Accepted Masons , in 1920, and has become a
major event in our s tate . • • ,"
The State Senate of Hawaii passed a Resolution respecting the 1966
Public Schools Week and included a commendation to the Masonic
Fraternity for sponsorship of this event.
Mayor John F. Shelley of San Francisco, and Sam Yorty of Los
Angeles, both issued proclamations. Mayor Yorty' s Proclamation made
reference to the California Grand Lodge.
These are mentioned only because of the geographical population
involved. Many others similarly contributed.
Communications were issued by P.G.M. Henry C. Clausen, 33° to
"All Valleys Orient of California" of the Scottish Rite, and by E. Mon~
roe Foster, Grand High Priest, Andrew F. Johnson, Grand Master, and
William D. Tucker, Grand Commander, to all York Rite bodies of
California.

166

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
GENERAL PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY

At the Committee's request the Masonic Press Club in LOs Angeles
disseminated large quantities of press releases and spot announcements
for radio and television prepared by the Committee. Similar material
was widely used elsewhere throughout the jurisdiction. In the future
it is intended that material will be made available to each committee man
who will see to the proper placement in his own territory.
Nine supermarket chains were contacted with the request that they
give Public Schools Week publicity in their ads the week preceding, and
also if possible, the week of Public Schools Week. Favorable replies and
advertising was received from four of the chains. It is hoped to increase
this in the coming year.
Postal meter die hubs were used by at leas t one public utility company in Southern California.
Several milk companies utilized Public Schools W eek imprinting on
their milk cartons.
Three half hour television programs devoted entirely to public
schools were produced. These dealt, among other things, with the history 0£ Public Schools Week and Masonic interest in the subject. The
Grand Master was the principal guest pa rticipant in one, the Senior
Grand Warden in another, and members of your committee took part in
two o f them. It is hoped to expand this type of presentation.
The 1966 posters and stickers were created a nd printed at Los
Angeles Trade Technical College, as in all recent years. This year the
California flag was reproduced on the posters for use in California, and
the Hawaiian flag for those distributed in H awaii.

Many lodges ordered and paid for these. A good many lodges did
not. Rather than destroy what was left on hand, supplies were sent
without charge to the lodges which had failed to send in orders. The
cost was charged against the budget of the Committee on Public
Schools. We recognize that a few lodges probably cannot afford to purchase the posters or do not have a need for the minimum order. Those
lodges which can afford the nominal cos t and which did not place orders, are urged to cooperate this coming year by joining in the program
and helping to defray the cost of printing which is done without any

1966 OBSERVANCES
We have received numerous letters, reports and programs of this
year's observance activities. They indicate that Public Schools Week
was widely and successfully observed in both states, and that many
excellent and well attended programs were presented. There is too much
detail to be included in this report. A voluminous file is being maintained,
and this can be made available for inspection by those interested. Much
help could be obtained therefrom by persons desiring ideas and suggestions.
Some lodges banded together to arrange large scale musical programs, and general programs with prominent speakers. DeMolays, Job's
Daughters, and Rainbow Girls participated in many of the programs.
Under sponsorship and guidance of a Lodge or Lodges, many schools
conducted essay contests. Winning essays were read on "Open House
Night" during Public Schools Week.
In the other classes, contests were conducted to see which room had
the most registered visitors on "Open House Night."
Prizes have been cash, honorary certificates, globes, dictionaries,
U . S. Savings Bonds, small hand looms, etc.
Incidentally, a $50.00 U . S. Savings Bond was presented, at an
assembly, to the art student at Trade Tech College who designed the
1966 Poster.
In the Barstow area, because of distances between schools and relatively small school population, the help of the U. S. Marine Corps was
enlisted to transport small groups by helicopter to a central meeting
place for a general program.
The optimum in lodge participation and attendance at observances
has not, however, been achieved.
We do not have an overall reliable survey, but we do have a sampling
by one of the committee members who sent out questionnaires to 109
lodges. He received only 73 replies. These showed that 57 lodges had a
Public Schools Week program, 16 lodges had none, and we have no
information as to the remaining 36 lodges which did not respond. This
is an unhappy contrast to areas where we know that participation was
virtually 100 %.

An innovation this year was the inauguration of meetings of the
entire Committee, attended by members from California and Hawaii.
Heretofore sectional meetings only had been held, in the interest of
economy, which we respect. However, we felt that general meetings
would be more productive in obtaining the coordinated ideas and forming

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The twenty-seventh annual report of the Grand Lodge of California
Committee on Constitution Observance that follows records the response by the Lodges in this jurisdiction to the Grand M.a ster's Proclamation, an account of the commendable accomplishments of the
Committee members during the past year, and our recommendation
concerning the status of this Committee for next year.
This year we observed the l 79th Anniversary of one of the most
ambitious and forceful documents ever written, the Constitution of the
United States of America.
Majority approval of the Constitution, foundation of our freedoms
and cornerstone of our Government. took place on September 17, 1787,
when thirty-nine of the sixty-five qualified delegates to the constitution
convention signed this document. Of the thirty-nine who signed the
Constitution, twenty-three are said to have been Masons.
At a meeting in Philadelphia under the Chairmanship of George
Washington, the Constitution was approved and sent to the Contin en ta!
Congress for submission to the people of the United States.
The Constitution Observance Committee was initially chartered as
a special Committee by Grand Master William B. Ogden in 1940 to
promote the observance of Constitution Day. This year Grand Master
Myron E. Smith chartered the Committee on Constitution Observance
as a Special Committee to assist Masons. their families and friends to
understand and appreciate the Constitution of the United States-to
show them that it is more than a mere historic document-that it is a
vital contract between each American citizen and his Government.
Most Worshipful Myron E. Smith in his proclamation dated June 1.

1966, pointed out that a grateful people have enshrined the Cons titution of the United States in the National Archives Building in the Nation's capitol. To stand before it is an unforgettable experience for here
is our charter of freedom and the heritage and pride of the American
people.
He also proclaimed the month of September, 1966, to be Constitution
Observance Month and directed all constituent Lodges in California and
Hawaii to hold public ceremonies during that month commemorating
the signing of the Constitution.
Your Committee is pleased to report that this year's Constitution
Observance was an unqualified success. Our aim was to promote awareness of our Constitution and appreciation of this great document.
Grand Master Myron E. Smith has sincerely and effectively supported his proclamation with dedication and enthusiasm. He w.a s the
keynote speaker at observance programs throughout the State.
The Grand Lodge of California was the leader among the many
fraternal. patriotic, and civic organizations joining together in public
ceremony to observe the anniversary of the signing of the Consti tution.
Analysis of the Masters' reports on the Constitution Observance
Program reveals the acceptance of the Grand Lodge assignment ranged
from acquiescence to enthusiastic support by the Lodge Masters. When
the Masonic organization did an outstanding job the people of California and Hawaii demonstrated interest in their program. Outstanding
observance programs were presented in the two states before audiences
ranging from a few score to several thousands. W~ especially co~men d
the Masonic Lodges sponsoring observances which were held m the
cities cited be]o,.,,. for they met our criteria of an outstanding program.
Although there were many other programs which are cons i~ered by
some to be even more impressive, these were selected for their overall
excellence.
