To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
Illness has deprived the Code Commission of its Chairman, Worshipful William Nankervis, Jr. He asked the Grand Master to relieve
him of his duties. The Grand Master, with his usual thoug htfulness.
allowed him to designate the Commission member who was to prepare
the report and thus the responsibility fell on the Vice-Chairman.
Great praise is due Brother Nankervis for his contribution to the
jurisprudence of the California Grand Lodge. He labored long, devotedly and skillfully to bring into being the California Masonic Code
and then to keep it current with annual annotations.
He commenced his work more than 10 years ago when he was
chairman of the committee created to revise the Ross Digest. It was
a happy choice. He possesses a wealth of experience concerning law
books and law editing. His name is know n throughout California as
the official reporter of the decisions of the California Supreme Court
and District Courts of Appeal.
Over the years, all members of the Commission have respected and
admired our Chairman's dispatch and efficiency and have appreciated
his never-failing courtesy and consideration.
The California Masonic Code was first published in 1956. It contained 434 sections, 1118 annotations and 200 pages of index. Cumulative annual pocket parts have been issued each year. The current pocket
portion consists of 88 pages setting forth 240 changes in the law by
repeal. amendment or new sections and annotations. This is almost a
book in itself wil:h a 23 page index.
It is apparent that the numerous changes should be integrated into
the Code. All repealed and superseded material should be eliminated. It
can be accomplished by a reprinting of the book.
When the Code was being planned, the Grand Lodge was told that
the annual pocket parts should keep the code usable for from five to ten
years. We have reached the maximum estimated. It is time to have a
reprinted Code integrating all changes to date. The project may be
expected to take a year, possibly longer. The Codes now outstanding
must be kept current by making pocket parts available to those who do
not desire the convenience of the new integ rated code.
The Commission has one additional recommendation and that is the
printing of a pocket~size inexpensive Code containing the sections of
the law without the cross-references, annotations or detailed index. It
is true that the annotations a.re valuable to the Masonic researcher in
showing the interpretation and application of the law by various Grand
Masters but a simple collection of the constitution and ordinances in
handy form, issued at small expense, would serve a valuable purpose
especially to beginning officers and interested sideliners.

174

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The publication of a code or annotated code is a self-liquidating
expense which can be funded through the office of the Grand Secretary
in the same manner as other Lodge supplies.
The usual pocket parts will have to be printed following this Communciation, thus keeping all outstanding Codes in working condition.
In the past, a small budget allowance has been set up for the use of
the Commission but we anticipate no travel or other expense during
the coming year and we ask that the allowance be discontinued.
We, therefore recommend as a matter of policy that the Code Commission be authorized to proceed with the publications herein described,
no new books to be released, however, until the contents have been
approved by the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and the Chairman of the Jurisprudence Committee.
Respectfully submitted,
EVERETT HOUSER, Vice Chairman

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The within report is submitted covering the stewardship of the Correspondence Committee of the Grand Lodge for the fiscal year 1965-66.
For the period commencing with the fiscal year 1954-55, and ending
with the fiscal year 1964-65, this Committee, in addition to its functions
of ·r eviewing published proceedings of Foreign Masonic Jurisdictions,
which include Masonic Jurisdictions of the United States, as well as
Masonic Jurisdictions of foreign countries and which are recognized by
the Grand Lodge of California, was responsible for the publication of
the California Freemason. This was an enjoyable task, as we have seen
this quarterly publication develop into one of the finest magazines of
any of the Grand Masonic Jurisdictions and it has been so accepted and
recognized.
We wish to pay our respects to the Grand Master, Myron E. Smith,
the Grand S ecretary, Edward H . Siems and their staff for their cooperation in making possible the reviews. In particular, we wish to pay our
respects to our former Chairman, Newcomb Condee, who is now Editor-in-Chief of the California Freemason, for his advice and counsel.
At the October, 1964, Communication of the California Grand
Lodge, legislation was adopted whereby the Correspondence Committee
was relieved of the responsibility for the publication of the California
Freemason, and this responsibility was placed under the direct supervision of an editorial staff, consisting of the Grand Master, the Grand

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

175

Secretary and an Editor-in-Chief. the latter to be appointed by the
Grand Master. Newcomb Condee, formerly Chairman of the Correspondence Committee, was appointed by the Grand Master as Editorin-Chief.
The Correspondence Committee is now giving its undivided attention to the review of proceedings of Foreign Masonic Jurisdictions, both
those within the territorial confines of the fifty states of the United
States, as well as foreign countries, and which in turn are recognized by
the California Grand Lodge.
There are 49 Masonic Jurisdictions in the United States, including
the District of Columbia, which issue official reports of their annual
proceedings, together with many jurisdictions of some 48 different foreign countries and which are fraternally recognized by the California
Grand Lodge.
Without enumerating the individual jurisdictions issuing annual reports, we are pleased to report that the Correspondence Committee has
reviewed all reports submitted by the various Masonic Jurisdictions to
the California Grand Lodge for the fiscal year 1965-66. These reviews
have in turn been submitted to the Editor-in-Chief for publication in
the California Freemason. Available space has not always permitted the
publication of all reviews submitted.
We trust that the reviews of Foreign Proceedings have been helpful
in editing the California Fteemason. These proceedings have frequently
been used as the basis of articles in the California Fteemason, in addition to the published short reviews.
Some of the •important problems, which are disclosed by a review
of the various Grand Lodge proceedings and have an unusual application
to all Grand Jurisdictions, may be said to be: The preservation of
Freemasonry's fundamental philosophy and landmarks in the light of
constant changes in the 20th Century, some of which are having an impact on Masonry in general and on individual Masonic Lodges in particular; the securing of stronger leadership in the Masonic Lodges to
the end that we can retain as Masons, those, who for various reasons
have neglected to keep their membership in good standing and at the
same time, create a renewed interest by all Masons in their Lodge activities; the welcoming into our Lodges of all Masons in good standing,
many of whom are sojourning Masons from other jurisdictions, but who
for sentimental reasons prefer to retain their original Masonic Lodge
membership in lieu of joining a new Lodge in a different jurisdiction;
making provision for a Masonic Home for senior Masons and their
wives, but who are not indigent. A successful answer to many of these
problems will remove the present vagueness of purpose in all too many
Masonic Lodges. These, as well as other activities of the Masonk Jurisdictions, are brought to the attention of the readers of the California
Freemason, many of whom are sojourning Masons.

J. BLOMSETH, GRAND ORATOR

Most Worship ful Sir. Honored Past Grand Masters,
Grand Lodge Officers and Member s, Distingu ished Guests and
Visitors, My Brethren All:
During this Masonic year it has been my privilege and great personal honor to serve at the will and pleasure of the Grand Master. And
at each ceremon y I have been asked to specify the duty of my office.

177

The: ritual provided my response and served as a constant reminder that
my prime assignme nt and responsib ility was, and is, the preparat ion
and tradition al delivery of the Grand Oration.
In accepting this office twelve months ago, I would confess that my
personal thoughts were poig~antly expresse d in t~?t weII known phrase
"Fools rush in where wise men fear to tread.
· · ·But, then, there can be no new experience without a certain amount
of risk. and if you please, a certain willingne ss to fail. For generally in
a new venture one finds little encourag ement in unsuppo rted and untried confidence.
But, as a magnificent contrast, in the work of Masonry we find
abundan t support and ·r einforcem ent. We discover anew that our faith
is founded upon an unwaver ing trust and confidence in the guiding force
of the universe , the Great Creator, who spake us into being. We learn
anew that the Supreme Architec t extends his beneficent grace to compensate weaknes s and to give strength and to spare when we are employed in useful and producti ve labor.
"For Such A Time As This", I was more than willing to accept the
challeng e and unequale d opportun ity to serve in one of the most rewarding assignme nts in all of Masonry .
In addition, and as unearned bonus. I was well aware that acceptance of this office would assure the continua nce of a dose associati on
with our Grand Master. An association which has included many miles
of travel, many hours of conversa tion and of breaking bread , and of
observin g him at labor in the vineyard s of Masonry . And the travel. the
conversa tion. and the observat ion have left an indelible mark of pure
inspiration. And who among us has not. in like manner, been inspired
by our Most Worship ful?
On behalf of the Grand Lodge Officers and Member s and of every
Master Mason in this jurisdiction, let the record show that our Grand
Master has proven himself to be (in his own words of admoniti on to the
craft) "possess ed with a consumin g concern for the welfare of othus"
and (in the language of his brethren ) "an elegant Christian gentlema n."
Thacker ay gives us a fitting definition: "To be a gentlema n is to be honest, to be gentle, to be generous , to be wise. and possessin g all those
qualities to exercise them in the most graceful outward manner." Such
a man is our Grand Master, Myron English Smith, truly. "an eleganl
Christian gentlema n."
I sincerely trust that he has found this officer's endeavo r acceptab le
and, if so. the credit shall rest with his continua l inspiratio n and magnificent leadershi p.
To borrow from the modern idiom, I have been " inflight" in Masonry just fourteen and one-half years. And when I view those highly
qualified. experien ced and distingui shed brethren who have held this
office before me. I am reminded of my youth and of my many deficien-

178

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

179

PROCEEDINGS O P THE

cies. And could not nor would not proceed with this present trust were
it not for the previously cited reasons and for the constant encouragement of my brethren, supported, as it were, by the declaration of William Pitt that eloquence is to be found "in the assembly, not merely in
the speaker."
I have selected as the title of this oration a single sentence from the
writings of Joseph Conrad: "There is no rest for a messenger till the
message is delivered."
The dominant theme woven throughout the literary works of Joseph
Conrad is the demoralizing effect of isolation. We. of the fraternity of
Free and Accepted Masons. can sympathize with Conrad's major characters, who sought to dispel loneliness in a vast sea of isolation, for we
are a society built upon the firm foundation of fellowship. We approached the door of Masonry as strangers, we entered as friends and
we became brothers in a world-wide society of men who possess like
knowledge and understanding. Fellowship is the very cement which
enables us to act in concert in the labor of ac<:omplishing Masonry's
one great and glorious goal-the Brotherhood of Man under the Fatherhood of God. And when this goal has been attainted both isolation and
loneliness will have disappeared.
For the next several minutes let us join in exploring and sharing
several immediate messages. As we proceed, it is essential that we
evaluate today's messages in the bright light of Masonry's ultimate and
supreme message, as we find it in the "emblem of truth overflowing",
the rule and guide of our faith, the open book upon our altar. Likewise,
that we keep in mind Emerson's provocative observation that "God offers every mind its choice between truth and repose."
Inasmuch as we are herein assembled as the Grand Lodge of California, it is appropriate that we select one of the implements of Operative Masonry to guide and to limit our discourse. The most suitable
implement seems to be the compass-that tool generally used to inscribe
360 degrees, with 32 points of division, and four cardinal points to mark
the direction of east, west, north and south. In Operative Masonry it is
that implement used for the admeasurement of the architect's plans, to
give those just proportions which assure beauty, as well as stability.
And in Speculative Masonry the compass is that implement most symbolic of virtue, the true and only measure of a Mason's life and conduct.
Let us figuratively pick up the compass that we might trace a few
lines upon the trestleboard of our understanding, to inscribe the four
cardinal points and a like number of messages. What shall constitute
today's messages? What are the messages that would be carried, without rest, to the point of delivery on this occasion?

THE FIRST MESSAGE-THE CARDINAL POINT EAST
A SOCIETY WITH SECRETS
One of the ma jor problems of our fraternity since its inception has
been how best to erase from the mind of the general public the idea
that Freemasonry is a secret society. Our great and beloved fraternity
was never designed to be in a ny sense a secret organization. T aken to
the extrem,e, to emphasize this very point, an American patriot, writer,
diplomat. signer of the Declaration of Independence, and a Past Grand
Master of Pennsylvania, W orshipful Brother Benjamin Franklin, stated
in one of his publications (just prior to his acceptance into the craft )
that Masonry's, " Grand Secret is that they have no Secret at all."
Certainly if this statement were true for the profane in Franklin 's day,
225 years ago, there is even less about the Masonic fraternity today that
is "secret."
Witness our well marked halls and temples (this debt-free California Masonic Memorial Temple. in particular): our lapel pins; our rings;
our announcements in the press; our numerous public ceremonies; our
magnificent homes at Union City and Covina (which inform the world
that the fraternity is ever mindful of the needs of those less for tunate ) :
and finally, the thousands-upon-tho usands of volumes of books , stories,
and articles (favorable and unfavorable) written upon every aspect of
Freemasonry and which can be found in every book store and libra ry in
the free world.
Obviously, what our good Brother Ben Franklin had in mind, and
rightly so, was to confirm that Masonry's membership, time and place
of meeting, activities, purpose and principles are well publicized and can
surely be well known to anyone having the slightest interest.
We were conceived, and remain to this day, an institution laboring
among men for the moral and social advancement of the whole human
family. If this be our purpose. and it is, then, how essential it is that we
carry the message to the profane, to the uninitiated, and to the entire
world that Freemasonry is not a secret society.
Undoubtedly the confusion on this point can be traced to our ri tual.
to our modes of recognition (whereby one of us may know another) ,
and to the private and confidential business of our tiled meetings. But
each of these is simply the universal secrecy which is recognized the
world over : that secrecy of the lawyer to his client, the minister to his
penitent, the physician to his patient, or of a friend to a friend. I t is
that trustworthy confidence which is present in every valuable rela tionship and is one of the foundations of the glory of man. W ithout it family, business. national and international rela tions would be imperiled, if
not destroyed.
Truly. the "secrecy" which Masonry maintains is that which is

180

181

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

practiced by all worthy individuals and is intended only to safeguard
the institution and to ensure its proper security.

Under the aegis of these two programs we endeavor to protect, secure, appreciate and understand the Constitution of the United States,
and to achieve and maintain widespread support for our free public
schools.
To describe these two Masonic programs in the simplest terms, we
annually make use of Brother Rudyard Kipling's six honest serving
men: their names, as you will remember, are-Where and What and
Why and How and Who and When.
You might well ask why we need be reminded every year, year after
year, decade after decade, of the necessity of supporting our free public
schools or of understanding our Constitution. The answer can be found
in the wisdom of a child's definition-"memory is the thing I forget
with!"
Unless we are constantly compelled to remember, we all too soon
forget, or what is far worse-we take it for granted-we assume. that
free schools and constitutional government are everybody's business and
therefore need not be our concern-and in a brief span of history, too
minute to measure, they become nobody's business-and they are gone.
The freedom we now enjoy was not easily won nor will it be so easy
to retain. Freedom demands of us the very best we have to give. And if
we would protect and secure our precious heritage, this free society, we
must willingly heed the advise of Episcopal Reverend Phillips Brooks,
who over 70 years ago delivered a prayer for all liberty loving people,
in these words:
"Do not pray for easy lives,
Pray to be stronger men.
Do not pray for tasks equal to your powers,
Pray for powers equal to your tasks."
Duty and responsibility must be constantly exercised by each and
every citizen or apathy will abruptly separate us from our precious freedom. Have we really delivered this message throughout our jurisdiction?
Can we rest till we have done so?

We are. then, a society possessing certain secrets, but not now nor
have we ever been a secret society.
Masonry has nothing to hide from the general public, it has no secrets beyond its rightful responsibility to confidentially conduct its private business. And there is a very valid reason why we must, each one
of us. deliver this message to all with whom we come in contact. I find
these few lines of Seneca's provide a comprehensive explanation:
"I will govern my life and my thoughts as if all
the world were to see the one and to read the
other; For what does it signif,y to make a secret
to my neighbor, when to God all our privacies
are open."
My brethren, the meaningful and significant work of Freemasonry
can not be accomplished without the aid and assistance of all right
thinking men. Masonry's one great, ambitious dream - the Brotherhood
of Man - Under the Fatherhood of God - rests upon the principle
of maximum participation. Is this not our first and most important message to all mankind? Can we rest till this message is delivered?
THE SECOND MESSAGE-THE CARDINAL POINT WEST
TO BE FREEMASONS
This current Masonic year our Grand Master has on several occasions reminded us of the significant fact that as a Grand Lodge and
through our constituent lodges we move into the public square and ask
for support with regard to two and only two Masonic programs: Public
Schools Week and Constitution Observance. What is the message here
that we would convey and why does it concern Masonry?
There is neither time nor opportunity this afternoon to trace the
birth and development of Freemasonry. But let us pause and note the
unquestionable fact that the process of evolution from Operative to
Speculative Masonry could only come from and with the great surge of
national endeavor which brought liberty to mankind at the end of the
Dark Ages. As our very name suggests, Freemasonry, in itself, embraces a desire to be and to remain free.
As we study the history of our fraternity, we are impressed timeand-again with the prerequisite of liberty. And when we have thoroughly
learned this lesson, we will have come to understand much, if not most
of the meaning of the free in Freemasonry. Hence. the undeniable importance of both our Constitution Observance and Public Schools We.ek
Programs.

THE THIRD MESSAGE---THE CARDINAL POINT SOUTH
INDIVIDUAL CRAFfSMEN

It has been said that '', .. a man's ideal like his horizon, is constantly receding from him as he advances toward it." So it is for every Master Mason, so it is for Masonry, and for all of mankind. But, here again,
Freemasonry possesses a most significant message. one which, tends to
elude each of us as we: translate our Masonic teachings into our daily
lives. It is the message of individual craftsmen.
The entire philosophy of Freemasonry is built around the individual
-the: erection of a moral edifice within the heart of a single man. All
our symbolism is pointed to the individual; all our traditions and prac-

182

PROCEEDINGS OP THE
GRAND LODGE OP Cl\LIPO.RNJA

tices are aimed solely at making individuals wiser, better and thus happier.
I have always found this single sentence of that eminent Master
Mason, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, to express in just seventeen
words, one of the most beautiful summaries of what we must do to earn
and warrant the title of brethren of the ancient craft: "Life is a quarry,
out of which we are to mold and chisel and complete a character." And
as a companion we might well add Michelangelo's lesson to the craftsmen: "The more the marble wastes, the more the statue grows."
If the objective of Masonry be the construction of moral edifices
within the hearts of men; if the objective of Masonry be thus centered
upon the individual-one man at a time; if such be our objective, then,
each one of us, alone, but well attended, must answer for himself that
ever-present question-"What is Freemasonry?"
As a reply, or if you will, as a personal message we might answer
that burning question as follows:
I belong to the fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons, which
encompasses the world within its walls; that can and does claim
the great and good men of every level of society; that discovers
with joy the gold in every creed; and floods with light and love
the goodness within every man.
Is it possible to "mold and chisel and complete a character" without
-concomitantly delivering a like message? Can there be. any rest for a
Masonic messenger till he has first formulated and then delivered his
personal message?
THE FOURTH AND FINAL MESSAGETHE CARDINAL POINT NORTH
THE SPREADING OF LIGHT
"No man, of woman born, coward or brave, can shun his destiny."
So spoke Homer in the 10th century B.C. What of Masonry's destiny?
What does the future hold for the true and trusty craftsman? Would
that one among us could respond for all. But any meaningful and lasting answer must come from the aggregate response of every Master
Mason.
How might we best respond? Let us begin with a single word to
guide our future acts as members of this great fraternity, :rnd let that
one word be enthusiasm. Emerson set forth its value as, "Every great
and commanding movement in the annals of the world is the triumph
of enthusiasm - Nothing great was ever achieved without it." Seeley
put it another way: "No virtue is safe that is not enthusiastic."
There is a story that became a legend in its time. A story that has
been told as happening in the Napoleonic Wars, although also reported
as having taken place in the American Civil War. Actually its origin is
of little import. It tells of a youth, too young to fight but who possessed

183

enthusiasm and devotion in such abundance that he was designated to
carry the regimental banner. During a bitter battle his unit advanced
slowly under heavy enemy attack. But his zeal carried him so far ahead
of the regiment that he was soon beyond hailing distance. His commanding officer sent a runner with the message - "Bring the standard back
to the line." The lad sent back the ringing reply - "Bring the line up
to the standard."
That particular story brings to mind with crystal clarity the advise
to our young Republic by Worshipful George Washington, in his Farewell Address: "Let us raise a standard to which the wise and honest
may repair.'' There can be no doubt that he would have wished his fellow Masons to find equal sustenance in his counsel!
Who among us can now envision the vast expanse of Freemasonry's
future attainments, if every Master Mason would but respond to the
challenge to "Bring the line up to the standard?"
My brethren, we are too deeply indebted to the founding fathers of
Freemasonry to accept in unthinking ingratitude what we have inherited.
Let us, each and every member of this great and good fraternity,
expand (if we now possess} or acquire (if we now lack) both a higher
opinion of ourselves and of Freemasonry - that we might travel forward on the firm faith of our convictions. Thus. and only thus, can we
assure that tomorrow will also witness its Masonic messengers!
Earlier, we figuratively picked up the compass that we might trace a
few lines upon the trestleboard to encompass, deliniate and mark four
messages:
The Cardinal Point East A fraternity possessing certain secrets - not a secret society;
The Cardinal Point West A fraternity exercising duty and responsibility in order to be and
to remain free;
The Cardinal Point South A fraternity of individual craftsmen:
The Cardinal Point North A fraternity employing dedicated and enthusiastic labor to ensure that its present and future attainments will ever reflect its
glorious past.
It is now time to close the compass, that implement most symbolic of
virtue, the true and only measure of a Mason's life and conduct, and to
return it to its proper place. May we do so with this observation: "There
are two ways of spreading light - to be the candle or the mirror that
reflects it."
The Grand Oration was received with a standing ovation.
The Grand Master directed the Grand Secretary to have printed
copies of the oration made available to the members of Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In addition to the type of activity which has been followed by this
Committee during previous years. a new assignment has been given
them in 1966. Under date of March 29 the Grand Master assigned to
this Committee the authority to "promote and correlate the work of the
Research Lodges." Part of the responsibility set forth in the Grand
Master's directive covered the reviewing of all material intended for
publication by the four Lodges involved.
The first step toward meeting this new responsibility was a planning
session at which the principle officers of the Research Lodges, with
members of this Committee, set up a schedule of guide lines. The steps
agreed upon were recorded as the procedures to be followed. A copy of
these "Procedures" is attached to this report as a matter of record.
The objective of the Committee during the past year, in the furthering of general educational activity, has been to emphasize the value of
greater knowledge of the fraternity to our newer members. At the same
time, older members have always been welcome to participate. We feel
that the holding of a number of group meetings and the formation and
encouragement of study groups under the leadership of Lodge chairmen
has measured gratifying progress in this field. Material for the use of
Study Groups has been forwarded to Group Chairmen with a letter encouraging them to seek further assistance from this Committee. We are
highly appreciative of the co-operation given us in promoting this part
of our activity.
The officers of the R~search Lodges have been very helpful in forwarding material which they contemplated publishing in accordance
with the established time schedule and in accepting the decisions of the
Committee where alteration or rejection of submitted material was necessary.
The reviewing of material submitted has involved a large volume of
correspondence. The help given the Committee by the Grand Lodge
office in meeting this situation is sincerely appreciated. Our thanks go
to the Grand Secretary, the Assistant Grand Secretary and the courteous and competent members of their staff.
We suggest that consideration be given to appropriating, for the
work of the Committee during the coming year, the sum of $2.000.00
plus such additional amount as will be required to cover enlarged activities which may be assigned to them.
Respectfully submitted,
HENRY D. OLIPHANT, Chairman
Referred to Committee on Finance.

PROCEDURES APPLYING TO THE DIRECTIVE ISSUED BY

The following details were fully discussed and mutually agreed
upon o~ April 23, 1966, by members of the Grand Lodge Committee on
Masonic Education (hereafter referred to as "the Committee") meeting
with representatives of the four Research Lodges (hereafter referred
to as "the Lodges").
( 1) No correspondence with the office of another Grand Jurisdiction shall be initiated by one of the Lodges, or by any member thereof,
except as based upon specific approval received from the Committee.
( 2} No material shall be published by one of the Lodges, either as
a separate paper or as part of a routine mailing. until such material has
been submitted to the Committee and approval thereof has been received
fro~ t?e ~ommittee. The term "published" applies to any material
which 1s prmted or otherwise duplicated for circulation and which can
in any way, be interpreted to indicate an opinion which is advanced a~
being M~so~i~ in. charact.er or as being held by a Masonic group as
such. This hm1tatlon applies particularly to statements of a religious or
political nature.
The above limitations do not apply to:
Correspondence from an individual member of one of the
Lodges forwarded to an individual member in another Jurisdiction.
Correspondence from one of the Lodges to a similar Lodge or
group u1 another Jurisdiction.
Published notices of meeting places and dates.
Schedules of available Papers.
Schedules of Masonic subjects for which speakers from the
Lodges are available.
Obituaries, notices of special events or similar items which do
not reflect a Masonic opinion.
( ~) The ro~tine for. approval, disapproval. or correction of any
submitted matenal shall include the. following steps:
. (a} E.ach of the Lodges shall have an official Screening Com~
m1ttee which shall review and clear all material before that material
may ~e forwarded for approval by the Committee. This screening
~ha!! 1~clude complete editing for spelling, punctuation and proper
md1catmg and crediting for any quoted material.
( b) Material shall be forwarded to the chairman of the Committee in triplicate and should be in his hands three weeks in ad~
vance of the time scheduled for being given to the printer.
( c} Material submitted for approval will be reviewed by at reast
two members of the Committee.
( d) After being reviewed by the Committeemen one copy of the

material will be returned with approval. or disapproval, and any
suggested corrections noted thereon. This reviewing and return will
be handled with all possible promptness. In extreme cases where the
question of the propriety of the submitted material is in doubt, the
materia l a nd question raised thereby will be submitted by the Committee to the Grand Master, or a Grand Officer designated by him ,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Cemeteries respectfully submits this annual report of their activities for the Masonic Year 1965-66.
We feel it wise each year to restate briefly for those new in attendance at Grand Lodge the purposes of this continuing committee. Our
duty is to care for those cemeteries under the direct care of the Grand
Lodge namely; Columbia State Park C emetery. Ja mestown Cemetery
a nd Fiddletown Cemetery. When called to our attention . we work w ith
indi vid ual Lodges where cemetery care problems exist and endeavor to
work out plans so the Lodges can care for them in a proper manner. We
see that any areas set aside in public cemeteries. for the exclusive use
of M asons. do not in their formation deviate from our laws with respect
to commercialism. On request, we recommend to the Grand Master for
his approval or disapproval with respect to propriety and conformity to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

187

Masonic law, any monuments or altars erected in such areas in public
cemeteries.
The activities of the committee will in this report be presented in
the order outlined above.
Columbia State Park Cemetery is under the Supervision of Committee member Marcel M. Baer of Sonora . Brother Baer has, for the
last two years, been able to have the work in the cemetery done by the
local group of the Future Farmers of America in the Sonora High
School. The committee wishes, in this annual record of activities, to expressly thank this group for their interest and cooperation in keeping
this historic spot in excellent condition for the public's enjoyment. You
will note. however, that in our budget request for the coming fiscal year,
we ask for sufficient funds to have any work at Columbia done through
conventional channels. This is necessary as we do not know how long
we can have the help of the Future Farmers of America group as their
plans change from school year to school year. Details of the work
anticipated for this cemetery during 1966- 1967 include, in addition to
the usual spraying for weeds and general care. the repainting of the
picket fence that surrounds the site. Doing this at this time will greatly
prolong the fence's useful life. Our budget request for Columbia this
year. including the $325 bid for painting the fence, is $75 less than last
year 's requirement.
Jamestown Cemetery, a lso under Brother Baer's supervision, was
rehabilitated during this last year. From an overgrown jungle of brush
and weeds, in which very little semblance of a cemetery could be discerned, has emerged another Mother Lode cemetery of historic value
that is a credit to Masonry. The site has been cleared and fencedheadstones have been repaired and replaced- aisles and paths outlined
and the entire plot presents a picturesque setting for Mother Lode
tourists. This year, a small amount of additional restorative work is
being asked for from Grand Lodge. W e would like to gravel the road
and aisles and erect a proper sign. When this has been done future
work will consist of general care at nominal cost. Our budget this year
requests sufficient funds to do this work and for general care. However,
with major work completed, our budget request is $940 less than last
year.
The cemetery at Fiddletown is under the supervision of committee
member Adrian Taylor of River Pines. Brother Taylor has worked hard
for several years to bring this cemetery to the condition it now presents
to the public. A small amount of additional repair work to headstones
and curbs remains to be done. A new gate to make accessible the lower
section of the cemetery is our only new construction requested for this
year. We do not foresee any further major construction for Fiddletown.
Our budget request this year is, therefore, $400 less than the 1965-1966

188

amount and we hope that future expenditures will be nominal and only
for general care and upkeep.
In our report last year we requested and received permission from
Grand Lodge to seek title to the historic cemetery at Red Dog. Red Dog,
east of Grass Valley, is adjacent to the largest collective hydraulic mine
in the world. The cemetery, about an acre in extent, is visited by people
from all over the world as evidenced by the guest book that has been
kept on the site by an interested brother, Lesslie Woodworth of nearby
Cedar Ridge. We were authorized by Grand Lodge last year to expend
up to $1000 in ·restoring this cemetery, providing absolute title was
given Grand Lodge and an access road provided. We also, with this
$1000, were given permission to place cement pads under headstones
at two other sites.
Title to Red Dog has not been given us as, while the owner is in
sympathy with our project, the property is for sale and he feels that
we should deal with the new owner. Our committee feels so sincerely
that restoration is desirable that we again, this year, are asking for permission and a budgeted amount to continue this work. Permission for
the cement pads was obtained and the work is scheduled, therefore the
request for Red Dog has been scaled down to eight hundred dollars.
Your committee respectfully requests that Grand Lodge at this time
again sanction this work.
Our other two committee members-Brother Harold C. Schroeder
in Sacramento and Brother G. Basil Gordon, Jr.. in Glendora-have
not had any problems arise in their areas and therefore have no individual reports for the Grand Lodge. As chairman, however, in compiling
this report I would like, if I may, to thank them for their cooperation and
help when called upon.
This year we have not been called upon to recommend sanctioning
of the formation of any areas in public cemeteries set aside for the exclusive use of Masons, nor have we been advised of any construction
projects in already established areas and therefore have not had to
review the erection of any monuments or altars.
We were asked by the Grand Secretary to investigate, for the Grand
Master, a reported difference of opinion in one of the Lodges with respect
to cemetery matters. After several meetings with brethren of the Lodge
associated with the cemetery management, and attendance at one stated
meeting, we feel that all issues were aired in a proper manner and that
the final decision of the assembled brethren was a fair and just one and
reflected honor on the Lodge and the Craft.
Our budget request for the fiscal year 1966-1967 to carry out the
work detailed in the foregoing report is as follows:

LOOKING AHEAD

. Your Library has now been in nominal existence for nine years, and
m actual operation for s even. We say "nominal" because when we
started we ~ad nothing of a physical plant and it was necessary not only
to create this but to overcome the opposition of some brethren who felt
other Grand Lodges were so far ahead of us that we should not even
try to establish a library.
We may comment on this that South Carolina, a considerably older
Grand Lodge than our o':""n· is even now inaugurating its Library and
we have been flattered with a request from it for information.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON DeMOLAY
To the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
It is gratifying to report that the Order of DeMolay is in fine shape
in the State of California. Great interest and much wholesome activity
is being evidenced. Although we find a great deal with which to be
pleased, we must note that the program is being carried out by relatively
a handful of very dedicated men and with inadequate financing. More
leadership and better financing could be used to great advantage.
Intelligent interest and support have been given by the Grand Master, Most Worshipful M y ron E . Smith, and his corps of officers. This
is deeply appreciated by those active in DeMolay .
The Order of DeMolay, being still young in years. having been
founded less than fifty years ago in Kansas City, has done well in
building better citizens. We know that throughout the world some
three million young men have knelt at DeMola'Y altars . We know that
a large percentage of these young men have become Master Masons
and leaders within their communities. It is also known that some sixty of
these young men have become Grand Masters of Grand Lodges.
In 1965, in our last ·r eport to you, the DeMolay Committee recommended that a special committee be appointed to study, in depth, and
make recommendations concerning some six specific needs of DeMolay.
With the strong interest being shown by appendant Masonic bodies
throughout the United States and particularly in California, your committee is pleased to learn that such a special committee is in the process
of being formulated by the Grand Master.
The DeMolay Committee feels that it has been fortunate in meeting with so many fine young people at their conferences and conventions. We also have had the privilege to witness the young boy who
has petitioned DeMolay and hearing him pledged to the Seven C ardinal
Virtues of DeMolay: Filial Love. Reverence, Courtesy, Comradeship.
Cleanliness and Patriotism.
In order to better assist these fine young men in bridging the gap
from boyhood into manhood, we strongly recommend a program of
action and support. With such additional action and support DeMolay
could easily double in strength and effectiveness. The individual members of this committee welcome the opportunity to meet with you and
your group to discuss the va rious aspects of DeMolay and perhaps
assist in having a DeMolay chapter exemplify one of its degrees before
your group. You are cordially invited to observe or attend the following:
Northern California DeMolay Convention, Sacramento - November 25-26, 1966.
DeMolay Traffic Safety Week (In co-operation with the California H ighway Patrol) - October 23-29. 1966.
DeMolayWe ek-March 12-18. 1967.

It is regretted that the Sojourner potential has not been recognized in
many areas and that so little effort has been expended to exploit that
po ten tia I.
We realize, in some areas, the Sojourners are few and far between,
but in most areas dilligent prospecting can and has produced surprising
results. The old saying, "You can lead a horse to water but you cannot
make him drink," applies in the quest for Sojourners. After the Sojourner is located and is invited to visit, a favorable climate must be
offered, for as stated in the 1963 Report of the Special Commission on
Masonic Practices, a favorable climate must be created to attract and
hold the visiting brethren as well as our own.
A study of Exhibit "A," attached, reveals that a favorable climate
has been created in many areas. The most productive areas were. not
limited to the metropolitan centers but included farming, mountain and
desert communities; communities where inspiration and encouragement, provided by Committeemen and Inspectors, has produced remarkable results.
Many of our Lodges had outstanding Sojourner affiliation records
during 1966, the most notable being: Consuelo No. 325 and Home
No. 721 with 12 each. These two Lodges were cited for outstanding
records in 1963, 1964 and 1965. A wonderful example of continuity of
effort. These Lodges are to be especially congratulated.

mention for their affiliations this year: Los Angeles No. 42 - 9; El
Cajon Valley No. 576 and Menorah No. 623 with 6 each and Ionic

during 1966: San Bernardino No. 348 and La Jolla No. 518 with IO
each; San Diego No. 35 and Hemet No. 615 with 9 each and Boron
U.D. with 8.
Two Masonic Districts have outstanding records for 1966: No. 644
at La Jolla with 20 and No. 638 at Lemon Grove with 16. These Districts
were cited in 1963. 1964. and 1965 for their affiliation records. This is
an illustration of what can be accomplished with a well developed program carried out with vigor.
The following Districts were cited in 1964 and 1965 for their outstanding records and again merit special mention: No. 520 at Burbank 21; No. 640 at San Diego -19; No. 516 at Van Nuys - 14 and No. 508

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SOJOURNERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
As our forefathers moved West to conquer the wilderness and carve
out a new nation, they carried the Bible with them and erected a church
for worship at every opportunity.
Included among these pioneers were Master Masons who carried
their Masonry with them and sought out and associated with their
brethren wherever found. New Lodges were formed at every opportunity.
Civilization, Religion and Masonry moved West together.
Today there is a great movement of population to California. Hundreds of Master Masons are included in this movement. All bring with
them the spirit of Mason r<y, but too often they fail to seek out their
brethren or an established Lodge. They soon become involved in their
daily activities and forget their Masonic ties. Thus, the active support of
hundreds are lost to the Fraternity. This is regrettable.
Your Sojourner Committee is aware of this tragedy and has endeavored to impress on the Office.rs of our Lodges the opportunity they
have to serve Masonry by seeking out the Sojourner, by offering the
hand of fellowship and by inviting the newly located Brother to visit
and participate in California Masonry.
Many of sur Lodges have developed excellent programs to rnund up
Sojourners, some of whom have affiliated with us. Many more have
failed to affiliate, for many reasons, but enjoy our Fraternal fellowship.

The above records reflect the leadership, the interest and the hard
work of the Inspectors and Masters of the respective Districts and
Lodges . All concerned warrant hearty congratulation s.
The Sixth Division is distinguished again this year for having at
least 1 Sojourner affiliation in each of its Masonic Districts for a grand
total of 266. The Fifth Division had the second highest number of
affiliations with 240.
Worshipful Brother Ben Salmon, who has the longest service
on the Committee and has been its most consistent worker, offers the
following comment relative to the success of the Sixth Division in general and of the southern half of the Division in particular: "The Lodges
are reporting increasing success of their respective efforts. The program
is not yet self sustaining however and requires the continued push of
active, militant members on the Committee."
The success in the Fifth and Sixth Divisions has been due to the
inspired efforts of the Committeemen , Inspectors and Masters in their
respective areas. Sufficient Committee coverage has not been provided
in other areas, however, to insure personal contacts to obtain the best
results. It has been found that personal contacts are worth many letters
and active leadership on the part of working Committeemen can do
much to insure the effectiveness of the Sojourner program. Serious
consideration to this conclusion is recommended. Active and inspired
coverage in strategic areas can do much to increase affiliations and
help reduce the decline in Grand Lodge membership, which is graphically
shown on Exhibit "B," attached.
Before closing , I wish to pay tribute to a Committeeman who labored
diligently to carry inspiration throughout the First Division. Worshipful
Brother William F. Jewett, Past Master of Chico Lodge No. 111 and a
member of the Sojourner Committee for 1964 and 1965 died at his home
in Chico on November 24, 1965. The Committee has lost a true friend
and a devoted worker. His enthusiastic service during this past year has
been missed.
Respecting the wishes of the Grand Master, expenditures were held
to a minimum during the past year and travel was drastically curtailed.
The Committee had a late start and this coupled with the curtailment
of travel and a reduction of coverage, contributed to the decrease of
Sojourner affiliations - 784 this year as against 922 last year.
To enable the Committee to publish a needed guide and other material for Lodges and to perform essential travel, an appropriation of
$2.000 is recom mended for the coming year.
We, who have had the privilege of working on this Committee, desire to express our appreciation for the opportunity to have been of
service and we extend our thanks to all who have given their coopera-

197

tion and support to the Sojourner program. Without the "grassroots"
effort, the results achieved would not have been possible.
Respectfully submitted.
DAV ID H . BLAKELOCK , Cha irman

Much attention has been given, the past few years. to the declining
membership of the Club. This is partially explained by the increased
on-campus activities offered by the University, and also the more intense
and consequently more confining courses offered. The University has
insisted that a high grade point average be maintained by officers of
all student organizations, sororities. fraternities, etc., and our Club
comes under that class~fication. During the past semester, several members of our student council were forced to resign from the council because they had not maintained the necessary grade point average.
The seriousness of the situation has been impressed on the present
dub membership, and, as a result, all members have dedicated themselves to publicizing the club, and giving more personal effort to securing
new members.
The University is inaugurating a new "quarter" sy stem effective with
the opening of college in September. This, in effect. means that the
college will have classes the year through.
Many of the members have spent a good portion of their summer
vacation securing from the University the names of the new enrollees
for the fall term. Brochures regarding the Club's facilities and activities
have been sent to these new students.
Our Board of Directors has an active Publicity Committee that is
striving to secure publicity through the various Masonic publications.
The events conducted during the year by the student council for the
members are many and interesting. There are get-together suppers.
dances. inter-club visits between Berkeley and ourselves, the annual
retreat which takes place between semesters-held this year at a private lodge near Big Bear, an annual Thanksgiving dinner for needy
children, an annual reception for the Grand Master, a joint Initiation
and Christmas party for parents, a Mardi Gras, a Spring Sing entry, etc.
These are but a few of the many activities planned each year by the
student council for members at relatively low cost.
Again, we appeal to you. the members of Grand Lodge, to visit the
two Clubhouses; to see what is offered the students and how we try to
provide the warm atmosphere of a "home away from home." Go back to
your Lodges and arrange visits to the Clubs. Let your members see what
Grand Lodge has been trying to do for the Masonic youth at the two
Universities. We feel that with this knowledge, the members will be
more conversant with the Clubs and can be more persuasive in having

their sons and da ughters become members. After all. it is to these young
people that we must look for the future leade rship of our Lodges.
Please cooperate with us, brethren, we need your help.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON COLUMBIA TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
During the past year the Columbia Temple was used by the Rainbow
Girls, DeMolay Boys and eighteen Lodges from various parts of the
state to confer degrees.
On the ground floor the Masonic Museum is now a reality. The two
glass bubbles and the display tables have been built.
On August 30, 1966, with the aid of the Columbia State Park Superintendent Neal Powers, Assistant Grand Lecturer Wallace H. Fiske
and Field Architect, Brother Buck R. Nelson, the steel doors that cover
the two glass bubbles were opened. The public may now view a small
but impressive display of early day Masonic artifacts which have been
loaned or given to the Museum by different brothers. A replica of a
Lodge room is set up with furniture that is over one hundred years old.
The Columbia Temple Committee realizing that the Temple is
used in the summer for degrees and wishing to provide comfort for the
visiting Lodges would like to replace the old air cooler, which is very
noisy and has to be shut off ·d uring degrees, with a more modern refrigerated air conditioner. This would be more efficient and would make the
visitations more enjoyable.
The following are costs of improvements which we would like to
make on the Museum during the year 1966-1967, also the flxed charges
and expenses:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC INFORMATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
We are happy to present a brief report on the activities of the Committee on Public Information.
The Public Information Committee reaffirms its premise that contact
with the press and radio (television) is the province of the local Lodge.
On this basis, the Committee has prepared and has published two sections of a Public Relations Manual which have been distributed to all
Masters. The first section is the booklet entitled, "If Freemasonry is
Good , Let's Talk About It," which you have all seen. It was written by
Past Grand Master Theodore Meriam. It expresses desirability of creating for our Masonic Fraternity an image of " Quality. Dignity and Substance." Should there be anyone who has not read this section of the
Manual. it is recommended that he do so at the earliest opportunity. The
second section of the Manual was prepared by the Los Angeles Masonic
Press Club. Past President W illiam Latta was the author. It is entitled
"Let's Talk About Freemasonry" and has also been sent to all Lodges
with the recommendation that it be read by every Master and every
Warden, and by members appointed to the very important Lodge Committee on Press Relations. It explains how to approach your local newspapers and radio-television stations to secure news coverage of events
being arranged by your Lodge. If you do not now have a copy. if you
have lost yours, or if the Master who preceded you did not pass it on ,
you may obtain another copy from the Grand Secretary's office.
A third section of the Manual is now being prepared and will be
published early in the coming year. It will consist of a series of carefully
written and edited sample news releases covering all the more common
situations in which your Lodge might become interested: Ins tallations,
Receptions , Public and Social Events, and so on. It is hoped that these
sample news stories will be of assistance to you.
A Public Relations or Public Information Seminar is planned for
February, 1967, to be held in Fresno. This seminar will be sponsored

204

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

jointly by the Public Information Committee, the Los Angeles Masonic
Press Club and the Northern California Masonic Press Club. Ma t
Masons interested in the .field of Masonic communication are inv~te~
to attend.
The Masonic Press Clubs, one in the South and one in the North
are active and productive. Membership in these clubs is not limited t~
~embers o.f the press and radio alone. It is open to all Master Masons
mterested m the field of public information.
Respectfully submitted,
WILLIAM H. ADAMS, Chairman

class round trip air rate of regularly scheduled major air lines, from
Honolulu to San Francisco, plus inter-island air fare to Honolulu when
necessary.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
OF THE MASONIC CLUB AT THE UNIVERSITY
BERKELEY, CALIFORNIA
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Your Board of Directors at the University of California Clubhouse
would like to preface our report with a plea for all of you to visit your
clubhouses, and see for yourselves that the picture painted by the few
who seek publicity, with banners and pickets and demonstrations and
wild parties. is not the true painting. The balance of the fine young
people seeking education to be our future teachers, scientists. doctors,
lawyers and political leaders comprise 98 % of the students. Do not be
afraid to send your sons and daughters to our state universities and
please do send them to your own clubhouses.
The Board has worked closely with the student council in making
every effort to stimulate membership and to give them one of the finest
clubs at U.C. We added several new reference books to our library and
a new complete Encyclopedia Brittanica; we also have a new calculator.
For the entertainment and comfort of the members we added a new
portable television, some new furniture and had our old furniture recovered.
We were again fortunate in having a fine group of officers on our
student council. The president. Jim Fonda, spoke at the Spring Breakfast of the East Bay Masters and Wardens and also at the Sacramento
Board of Relief Spring Breakfast. Those of you who were privileged to
hear this young man speak and to see and talk to him have a good picture of the type of young people your Masonic Clubs attract.
The general administration of the clubhouse by M:rs. Janice Kohl was
excellent, and the social activities under the direction of Mrs. Mary
Kierulff were interesting and well attended. We were especially pleased
to entertain our busy Grand Master and Mrs. Smith with a reception
and an initiation ceremony during the spring term.
Your Berkeley Clubhouse is situated in one of the urban renewal
areas. We are pleased to announce that our building improvements exceeded the recommended expenditures and the building passed the inspection by the bureau.
At the request of the Grand Master, our by-laws are being changed

REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTE E ON DEFINITION
OF COMMITTE E RESPONSIB ILITIES AND
CODE REVIEW
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Grand Lodge having previously approved the creation of such
a committee, the Grand Master, on March 11, 1966. appointed five
members to this committee and designated four ex officio members.
One reason for the authorization of such a committee is the absence
in the California Masonic Code of any specification as to the responsibilities or sphere of most committees of this body. As an example, section
192 of the code requires the Grand Master to appoint 118 members to
14 committees named therein. but the following sections specify the
responsibilties of only five of the 14 committees. Elsewhere in the code
there are scattered sections as to other committees. It appears reasonable that these provisions should be brought together and not left
scattered.
Another reason for the authorization of this committee was the
opinion, expressed by several recent Grand Masters, that the code as a
whole needed updating.
The first task undertaken was a draft of proposed sections as to 19
committees. as to titles, number of members and the scope of responsibility of each. This has been completed. It would have been physically
possible to have had these circulated with the more than 40 resolutions
circulated in August, but the committee decided to defer presentation
of any proposed amendments to the code until the next annual communication. at which time, it is anticipated, a substantial number will be
presented by the committee.
It should be stated that one of the major purposes of the committee
is to couch the sections of the code in language which should be easily
understood by any reader regardless of professional training. Another
aim is not to use a single word more than is absolutely necessary. We

209

believe we have achieved these aims thus far. At the time of presentation
cogent reasons will be given for any changes of phraseology which may
be proposed.
I move that this report be received and filed.
Respectfully submitted.
ELLSWORTH MEYER, Chairman

Referred to Committee on Finance.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON OLD MASONIC HALL
IN LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
It is most gratifying to report to you again as Chairman of the
Committee on Old Masonic Hall in Los Angeles. The Hall is still open
only on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays from 12 noon until 5.00 p.m.
Brother Joseph Wray Gibson is still the custodian and I would like to,
state here that he is a fine representative of our Temple. Brother Gibson ,
with his fine old ways, is an integral part of our Temple and he is part of
the scenery, giving the visitors a good impression of old time Masonry.
Plaza de Los Angeles Lodge No. 814 is the only Lodge that meets
in our Old Hall. Any Lodge can use the Hall for any special event that
they may choose. but few have taken advantage of this excellent opportunit·y to present to their members this genuine image of Masonry in its
beginnings in Los Angeles.
During the past year approximately 2650 members of our Grand
Jurisdiction visited the Old Masonic Hall in Los Angeles, 100 of Foreign
Jurisdictions, 600 from other Grand Lodges in the United States. plus
2500 visitors from California, the United States and many foreign countries. The grand tota l of visitors for the past year totaled 5850.
Recently new monies have been allotted by the State of California
for continued restoration of the Plaza de Los Angeles, of which our
Hall is a part. Some of this money has gone for the completion of our
back stairway and the balcony that surrounds the Hall. When the entire
project is completed all the exhibits will be open s ix days a week. The
Committee feels that the budget for the Hall should be increased to
$1500.00 for two reason~: First. that our Custodian's hourly wage be
increased and, secondly, we must be prepared to be open six days a
week in conformity with the other buildings in the area.
Referred to Committee on Finance.
Respectfully submitted,
BENJAMIN M. WFJss. Chairman

MORTGAGE BURNING CEREMONY
Masons, their friends and interested persons were a dmitted to the
auditorium to witness the ceremony of burning the mortgage on the
California Masonic Memorial Temple. Special guests included the architect, the builders and the representatives of the banks holding an interest
in the mortgage.
The symbolic ceremony represented the culmination of the efforts of
all the members of the jurisdiction. A sense of pride and satisfaction in
reaching this fraternal milestone was felt by all present.
The ceremony in its entirety is printed below.

ORGAN PRELUDE
Music by Octet
RITUAL
GRAND MASTER (calls to order)
From the beginning of time men ha ve been builders. The earliest
man firs t lived in natural caves but eventually he built his own dwelling
of stones, of bones, of hide, of twigs and branches. Through the centuries man became more adept and experienced. His buildings grew in
height and stability and eventually in beauty. As man became more
civilized and began to reason, he realized that there were forces and
phenomena beyond his comprehension and understanding.
It became his nature to fear that which he could not understand and
finally fear turned into a form of worship by which the forces he experienced, but did not understand, would be appeased and pleased. Sacrifices
of food and other important worldly possessions were offered-first on
altars in the open and then enclosed in temples.
And so it is that over thousands of years man has constructed temples and cathedrals, palaces and public buildings and these have taken
major space in the history of art. Even from the dawn of history the
art of building has so consistently touched and mingled with human life
in the home-in the shop---in the temple-that it has often become the
best history and commentary of the times.
Today the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California has met for the purpose of celebrating
the completion of a resolve which originated eighteen years ago.
In 1948 men of experience began to have visions of a Masonic Temple of great beauty--erected to God and dedicated to M asons who gave
their lives that we might live a last measure of devotion to the holy cause
of liberty.
That dream began to take form and substance in a site-in sketches
and then in working drawings- in steel and concrete-in stone and glass
-in fine wood-and in skilled workmanship.
Contributions which Masons of California and Hawaii had made

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

211

toward a memorial honoring their fallen dead were converted into brick
and mortar. Voluntary donations began to flow in from all over California and Hawaii and members of the Grand Lodge agreed to a stipulated assessment. Finally six San Francisco banks, as a great example
of faith in the promise and integrity of this Grand Lodge completed the
financing of California Masonic Memorial Temple with loans totalling
more than $2.300,000.
Now eight years and fourteen days after the dedication of a dream
accomplished we meet to commemorate the fulfillment of a pledge-a
promise made earlier that the faith and confidence represented by the
extension of credit would be justified.
In accordance with the teachings of our institution. it is our duty
before entering upon any great or important undertaking , to invoke the
aid and blessing of God. We sha ll therefore reverently unite with our
Grand Chaplain in an address to the Throne of Grace.
GRAND CHAPLAIN: (Prayer)
GRANO MASTER:
Brother Grand Secretary, you will read a summary of the events
which have brought California Masonic Memorial Temple through the
stages of planning, building , completion, financing, and to the fulfillment
of the pledge to retire all debt.
GRANO SECRETARY:
Most Worshipful, in the 98th session of Grand Lodge convened in
1947 Grand Master John Moore gave the real impetus to the b uilding
of the temple when he said,
" In addition to serving as a memorial to our brothers who served
and died in World War II a new Temple would furnish a comfortable meeting place for the delegates to our communication in
the years to come and would provide a fitting place in which to
pause and acknowledge our debt to the early builders of Masonry
in C alifornia whose consummate wisdom, fidelity. and courage
have placed in our hands this magnificent heritage."
During the entire year of 1948 a special committee investigated locations, building costs, and financing. The study extended through the
years of 1949, 1950, and 1951 when Grand Lodge approved a per capita
tax of 50¢.
In 1952 the per capita was raised to $1.00 and an architect was
employed.
1953 was the year of action. Grand Master Arthur Warren called a
special conference of Past Grand Masters, elected Grand Lodge Officers
and standing committee chairmen to review the Temple Committee's
recommendations to be made to Grand Lodge. G rand Lodge approved
a contribution of $9.00 from each applicant for degrees.
In 1954 it became apparent that the Masons of California were clear

( C) JUNIOR GRAND WARDEN approaches the crucible and stands to the
South. He pours the contents in the crucible.
GRAND MASTER: (Comes down from the East and joins with the Grand
Marshal in approaching the crucible from the East. The Grand Marshal
stands to the left and rear of the Grand Master holding the ignited lamp
and tray.)
All of the performances of human art at which we look with praise
and wonder are the result of the resistless force of perseverance. By this
virtue the quarry becomes a pyramid. The first turn of a spade is overwhelmed by the final result. yet each petty and seemingly insignificant
operation incessantly continued in due course of time surmounts the
greatest difficulties.
Thus through the continuing and determined efforts of the Masons
of California and Hawaii the quarry has supplied the demands created
by the first turn of the spade.
Dreams and ideas h;:ive manifested themselves in development and
labor. Earth has produced stone and iron to which the architect and
builder applied the sciences of geometry. chemistry and physics. Thus
this Memorial Temple arose. dedicated to God and honoring those who
served their country with faith and courage and with a willingness to
make the supreme and final sacrifice that the ideas and principles of freedom might be forever preserved. The faith which the business community had in the integrity and honor of the fraternity has now been justified . The debt has been paid in full. The pledge of more than 220,000 men
and Masons has been redeemed.
"We have fought the good fight, we have finished the course, we
have kept the faith."
(GRAND MARSHAL passes lamp to GRAND MASTER who lights the fire.)
Music: "Bless This House"
(Officers return to stations at end of music.)
GRAND MASTER:
The Grand Chaplain will now give the benediction which will conclude the ceremony.
GRAND CHAPLAIN:
May the blessing of Almighty God, Who made the heaven and the
earth, and all who dwell therein, be with us all and remain with us, now
and forevermore. Amen.

CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
PER CAPITA (C.M.C. SEC. 283)
T o the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, as a result of a recommendation made by the Special
Committee on Memorial Temple in 1953, the Ordinances of Grand
Lodge were amended by its action to make effective the allocation of

NOTE: Leo E. Anderson, P.M.• No . 355, as a member of the Committee on Jurisprudence, did not sign the above legislation but submitted.
as a minority report, Resolutions Nos. 37, 38, 39 and 40. Resolutions

Nos . 37, 38 and 40 were subsequently withdrawn. Resolution No. 39

Th~. Committee on Jurisprudence made the following explanatory statement:
G. M. Theodore Meriam appointed a Special Committee to study
the use of liquor as it relates to Masonry. The report was rendered at
the 1965 Communication and the recommendations of the Committee
were adopted by the Grand M aster in his Annual Message as his own
recommendation. The Grand Master ref erred the report to the Jurisprudence Committee to draw the implementing legislation for this 1966
Communication. This we have done with the assurance of P.G.M. Phil
Meyers, Chairman of the Special Committee, that the proposed resolutions which the Jurisprudence Committee has prepared does carry out
the recommendations of his Committee.
Briefly stated, the Special Committee clarified and liberalized the
provisions of the Masonic Code relating to the use and sale of liquor in
the following material respects :
(I } The membership of Masonic lodges and that of concordant
bodies (i.e .. organizations requiring that their members be Masons) a re
to be allowed to serve and consume intoxicating liquors at social affairs
or meetings in hotels, restaurants or other establishments serving liquor.
Also, open installations may be held in such places but no liquor is to be
consumed or served during the installation ceremony itself. Furthermore,
the Grand Master must approve as suitable the location of any Blue
Lodge installation.
( 2} Masonic Temples or temples of concordant bodies may be
located and meet in buildings where bottled liquors are sold as incidental
to other businesses as in a grocery store, unless the advertisement of the
liquor is offensive or dominates the exterior advertisement of the building. Also, if a lodge inherits property having a prohibited use or, in good
faith, is burdened with an offending lease. the lodge is given the reasonable time required to rectify the situation.
( 3) A bartender or one in the bar business may apply for the degrees
of Masonry and will be judged by the same standards as any other
applicant, i.e .. on his merits and not by his means of making a living so
long as his business is lawful.
( 4} The membership of all Masonic related organizations in this
jurisdiction, i.e., those requiring that members be M asons, shall be governed by the same rules of conduct and propriety as is required of Blue
Lodge members in this jurisdiction. There are to be no classes of Masons
in this regard.
( 5} California Masons while in other jurisdictions will abide by the
practices, policies or laws of those jurisdictions and a lso the practices,
policies or laws of the California Grand Lodge which are not inconsistent
therewith. Masons of this jurisdiction, whether they live in the jurisdic-

224

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

tion or outside, must do nothing within this jurisdiction contrary to the
Masonic law thereof.
There are refinements to these general statements. as you will note
when I read the proposed resolutions. However, I have indicated the
signiflcent changes. As I stated before, I have been assured by P.G.M.
Phil Meyers, Chairman of the Special Committee, that we have effectuated the Special Committee's recommendations. I again repeat that the
Jurisprudence Committee is making no recommendation but is merely
carrying out its mandate to prepare the legislation and we will move the
adoption of the various resolutions for the purpose of placing them before Grand Lodge.
Other resolutions are being offered. As their proponents will no doubt
point out, these resolutions go farther than the G.M.'s and Special Committee's recommendations in liberalizing the present rules on the use of
liquor. They would permit concordant Masonic bodies to serve liquor in
their temples or regular meeting places. Some would allow the renting of
Blue Lodge social halls to organizations which may serve liquor at their
affairs held in the Masonic Temples. and some would go so far as to
permit liquor to be served at the Blue Lodge's own social affairs held in
the social halls of Masonic Temples. I merely mention these alternatives
to apprize you in a general way of the nature of legislation proposed by
others than the Special Committee.
It is apparent that these subsequent resolutions proposed by others,
in all respects in which they do not agree with the Special Committees
resoluions, are clearly inconsistent therewith, and the passage of any
one of the Special Committee's resolutions will obviate the necessity of
voting on any of the other resolutions covering the identical issue.
NOTE: The proponents thereafter withdrew Resolutions Nos. 37,
38, 40, 41, 42, 43 and 44.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Proposed Resolution No. I seeks to place in the California Masonic
Code clear permission and authority for discussion in Lodge meetings
of matters pertaining to the welfare of public schools locally as well
as statewide. Section 331 C.M.C. permits discussion in a Lodge meeting
of statewide public schools welfare. However the California Masonic
Code is silent as to the discussion of local public schools welfare within
our Lodge meetings. Most Lodge officers have considered such discussion as being improper because they have deemed public schools issues,
which are to be voted upon by the voters of a school district. as political
in nature and thus banned from discussion in a Lodge meeting. For the
past 47 years the Masons in California have sponsored Public Schools

MASONIC TEMPLES FUND
(3)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It is proposed to all the members of Grand Lodge that a perfectly
good way to assure that a Lodge desiring to build a new Templ.e, ~o~ld
accomplish this desire by an assessment of each member of the Jurisdiction for $1.00 per member per year, this would create in one yea r a Fund
of over $250.000.00 and this amount would be increased by that sum
each year, then as a n ew or old Lodge or even a small group of ~od~es
made known their desires to build a Temple they could make apphcat10n
for a loan on an interest free basis to the above mentioned Grand Lodge
Fund who would take a Mortgage on the newly proposed Temple. repayment can be made the same as a homeowner pays his mortgage off.
just like rent; and
WHEREAS. There is a great need for such a "Fund" since many
small Lodges are sometimes required to exist in a "less than desired"
condition for many years before they are able to realize their dreams of
having a "Home" of their own; and
WHEREAS. the reason for this condition, is that not too many
Masons are rich enough to donate large sums to their own Temple Funds
a large enough amount to do the job adequately, especially with constantly rising land prices and building costs. Temple Associations are
finding that even if they find a choice piece of land at a reasonable price,

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

231

it may be sold or the price jumps up by the time the Lodge Members can
scrape up enough money to buy, thus Masonry in that Lodge is thwarted
by conditions beyond its control; a nd
WHEREAS. when we face the facts, there are very few ways that
a Lodge can legally raise: funds and still maintain the dignity of Masonry
as is required by Grand Lodge, and then the few dolla rs raised legally
are so paltry that the Brethren become discouraged in such a slow attempt to raise money that they soon falter; and
WHEREAS . it is well known that "Success Begets Success" and if
Masonry, all over California, could put forth a more prosperous front by
being able to build in a community, a Temple compatible with many
other well known institutions, then Masonry in this state would more
properly reflect a successful image to the community in general; and
WHEREAS. the proposed "Fund" would constantly grow each
year and while it would fluctuate by the va rious loans made against it,
the fact becomes obvious that after a few years it would become large
enough that by the same prudent investment, as the HOMES ENDOWMENT FUND of the amount not being used the dividends themselves
would provide enough to operate on, and in the some distant future such
assessment could be dropped. but in the meantime such assessment for
most Masons would be hardly felt, surely most of the Masons feel
enough pride in their Fraternity to give the insignificant sum of $1.00
per year to help put Masonic Lodges into proper Masonic Temples
which every Mason can point with pride, it is certainly a small enough
amount to ask.
THEREFORE . BE IT RESOLVED : That beginning with January

his regular dues which shall be an assessment to be held in a separate

by existing Advisory Committees, all such payments by the Lodges to
be adjusted by the individual Lodge's ability to pay (such as size of membership and annual income of Lodge) and over the necessary period of
time required in accordance with the amount of the Loan.

actual costs to the Lodge making such Loan with such costs to be kept at
